Business.title: Energy bills to rise by 26% from January after gas prices surge
Business.text:
Energy bills will soar by 26% for millions of households in January after a surge in gas prices sparked by the Iran war.

A typical bill will increase by about £37 a month in the first three months of the new year, although the price will depend on how much energy a household uses, so it could be closer to £60 extra a month in winter.

A household using a typical amount of energy in England, Scotland and Wales and paying by direct debit, would see their annual bill rise from £1,723 to £2,166 if the increase was sustained for a year, said regulator Ofgem.

The government will pay millions of households £100 from 4 January to help cover winter costs on top of an existing VAT cut on electricity.

Charities and suppliers expect debt to rise and a wave of people to need emergency support.

Ofgem said the rise had been driven entirely by higher wholesale costs faced by suppliers owing, primarily, to the Iran war. Wholesale gas prices, paid by suppliers, were up 33% in the last three months, the period used to set the January to March cap. They have more than doubled since late 2025.

The warm home discount will take £150 off bills for six million households on benefits this winter. There have been calls for this support, funded through everyone's bill, to be extended.

"We are staring down the barrel of a brutal winter," said Dame Clare Moriarty, chief executive of Citizens Advice.

Neil Kenward, Ofgem's director general for markets, said it wrote to energy suppliers "reminding them of their responsibilities" to customers this winter. They have been told to identify people who need help early, make support easy to access and ensure repayment plans are affordable and sustainable.

Campaign Groups Friends of the Earth and Global Witness said major oil and energy companies are making huge profits because of spiralling oil costs, hurting households.

Energy UK, which represents suppliers, said the firms which send your bill, have profits capped on a percentage basis and do not see the same benefit as international energy generating companies. However, higher bills will mean higher profits in nominal cash terms.

The increase is the biggest since Russia's invasion of Ukraine drove up prices. It comes at a tough time of year, when the weather is at its coldest.

People on prepayment meters will be hit as their spending comes when energy is needed, rather than the cost being spread over the year as with direct debits.

The cap sets a maximum price for each unit of energy, not the total bill. Those on fixed deals are unaffected until the end of their term, but for those on variable tariffs it means:

For electricity, average unit prices will go up on 1 January from 26.32p per kilowatt-hour to 32.69p. The electricity price is often pegged to gas, owing to gas-fired generation.

Gas will increase from 7.97p per kilowatt-hour to 10.96p, higher than in the wake of the invasion of Ukraine.

Daily standing charges will be 54.77p for electricity and 29.65p for gas.

The cap is set every three months, based on the costs faced by suppliers as well as the cost of running the energy system.

It is based on a three-month period that ends about six weeks before the new cap comes into force. A fall in international wholesale prices in recent days will not be reflected in January's cap, but it will be in April's.

Energy Secretary Miatta Fahnbulleh said people will be "deeply concerned" by another rise in energy bills.

"For too long, British families have been paying the price for conflicts overseas and volatile fossil fuel markets," she said.

Andrew Bowie, shadow energy secretary, said: "It is an outrage that, as bills soar, Labour are not only piling green levies and taxes onto bills but signing us up to an EU scheme that risks pushing them even higher.

Up to 20 million households in England will get a £100 payment from 4 January to help with their energy bills this winter, with equivalent payments in Scotland and Wales.

Citizens Advice said the money will disappear quickly, particularly for those on prepayment meters, leading to a wave of requests for emergency help.

Energy UK said the funding was poorly targeted and insufficient to stem rising levels of customer debt.

The government said councils had a £100m discretionary fund to support vulnerable households which fell outside of the main scheme.

Business.title: Energy bills will soar - here's how you can save energy to ease the pain
Business.text:
Energy bills will soar by 26% in the new year as the war in Iran pushes up wholesale prices.

Typical household bills will rise by £37 per month as Ofgem's latest price cap comes into force from January to March, but experts say it is possible to keep rising bills in check.

Here are four areas to consider ahead of the increase.

Ofgem's price cap, as well as suppliers' fixed deals, set a limit on the price of each unit of energy, not the total bill.

So, you pay for what you use. Millions of people have cut back on their energy consumption during years of relatively high prices.

With the unit price of gas, in particular, set to soar, experts say you should take a fresh look at your energy use and renew good habits.

Research foundation Nesta suggests:

turning down the flow temperature on a combi boiler - usually indicated by a radiator icon, to make it operate more efficiently

turning off the pre-heat facility on some combi boilers, which would have kept some water heated up when not in use

turning down the thermostat one degree, although 18C is the recommended minimum

closing all curtains at night

lowering radiator valves outside of the living room

turning off the heating before April

These are small changes but - alongside washing clothes at 30C, blocking draughts and batch cooking - they can reduce energy use and bills.

Ofgem says about five million people still pay their bill when it arrives every three months, rather than receive a monthly bill often initially based on an estimate.

Taking regular meter readings, or having a smart meter, while paying by monthly direct debit solves that problem.

Paying by direct debit costs significantly less than by so-called standard credit - typically £138 cheaper a year.

Customers on prepayment schemes - usually people on low incomes struggling to pay bills - used to pay a higher rate than others, but now they pay slightly less than the capped direct debit variable rate.

Various deals may rely on paying by direct debit or having a smart meter.

Moving to a fixed energy tariff means the price you are charged per unit of gas or electricity does not change every three months, although the total bill will still vary depending on how much energy you use.

The trouble is that it is very difficult to work out whether a fixed deal is a good deal at the moment, for those renewing fixed deals or looking for one for the first time.

Some fixed deals are available at unit prices below the next forecast price cap level. But should energy prices fall sharply then a longer-term fix might not seem such good value compared with the price cap.

So consumer group Which? also recommends paying close attention to any exit fees when picking a fixed deal. If variable prices fall below your fixed rate and you want to get out of it before the end of your agreement period, you may have to pay a hefty sum.

Before you fix, consumer website MoneySavingExpert advises you look at all the deals available, not just what your own supplier is offering.

The government will give a £100 payment to millions of homes to help cover winter energy costs. It will go to homes in council tax bands A to D in England, with the equivalent expected in Scotland and Wales.

There are also a range of other forms of support specifically for people on low incomes.

This winter anyone on means-tested benefits will get £150 off their electricity bill.

Your supplier will apply the discount automatically unless you are in Scotland, where you will need to contact your energy company to ask for the help.

Some people will also be eligible for a Cold Weather Payment, external and most pensioners will receive the winter fuel payment.

Beyond that, most energy suppliers offer hardship grants for people struggling to pay their bills and the government's Fuel Direct Scheme, external can help you repay energy debt.

You can get more advice from Ofgem, external, Citizens Advice, external, or your own energy supplier. Trade body Energy UK has a list of support schemes, external.

People on low incomes may also be eligible for grants to help with insulating their homes, and there are local schemes offering grants for solar panels, heat pumps and the like.

But if you are hunting around for grants, watch out for scams pretending to be official money-off schemes.

Business.title: 'I only use the washing machine on a Sunday' - how we're keeping our energy bills down
Business.text:
Domestic energy prices will soar by 26% in January under the regulator Ofgem's new price cap, pushing up bills for millions of households across England, Scotland and Wales.

With household budgets already under pressure, finding ways to reduce gas and electricity costs has become increasingly important. But how much difference can simple changes really make?

The BBC spoke to three people about what they're doing to keep their energy costs down.

Like many people, Kelly Anne Harvey, a building surveyor from Cleveleys near Blackpool, is worried about her energy bill going up next year.

The 44-year-old, who is married with a five-year-old son, has a combined household income of £60,000.

She currently pays about £154 a month for gas and electricity on a standard variable rate with Octopus, but is looking for a fixed-rate deal to offset the rise.

The family fell into arrears on their energy bills a few years ago and Kelly says she won't let it happen again.

To control her costs she pays by direct debit, which spreads her payments and is typically £138 cheaper a year than paying on receipt of a bill.

The family uses electric blankets and portable oil radiators in some rooms so they don't have to turn the central heating on as often.

They also take part in Octopus's energy saving scheme, which rewards customers who use less electricity at peak times, such as early evenings, with a free hour of energy at the weekend.

"On Sunday we'll turn on the dishwasher, tumble drier, washing machine and maybe even charge our electric cars," says Kelly.

Stacey, 40, a single mother from Bristol, says dealing with rising energy costs has felt like a "battle" recently and she's worried about 2027.

The office worker, whose daughters are aged 10 and 12, is on a fixed-term tracker tariff with E.On Next, which charges rates set below the quarterly Ofgem price cap. She expects to pay £1,800 for energy this year, up £400 on last year.

Stacey, who is part of the Changing Realities project at Glasgow University, which documents life for people on low incomes, has tried a number of things to control her energy costs.

She's turned her central heating down from 22C to 19.5C, bought electric blankets and pays her bills by direct debit.

She also leaves her curtains shut to "keep the heat in", while her daughters wear thermal clothing if it gets chilly in the house. The family is also using less hot water.

"I've got girls and they're growing up and they want to spend loads of time in the shower [but] it's just not possible."

Around 1.5 million households in the UK rely on heating oil for heating and hot water, and their costs have already soared in the past year due to disruption in global oil markets.

"When I first moved here two years ago you could get a litre of heating oil for 50-60p," says Bradley Knowles, 32, who lives in a barn conversion with his husband, mother and sister in rural Lincolnshire.

"At the height of the Iran war it went up to £1.20 or £1.30 and now it's stabilised at around £1."

To cut costs, the finance worker orders oil in bulk, buying 1,000-1,500 litres, preferably in the summer months when prices are lower. He also tries to order a few weeks in advance to avoid expensive next-day deliveries.

Bradley uses comparison sites to see which local suppliers offer the cheapest oil and puts money aside each month so he can always afford his orders.

Oil-powered boilers may take time to heat up, but Bradley advises against leaving them on all day as that can be very expensive.

Instead, he uses an electric tank to store his warm water and tops up the heating in parts of the property with electric radiators.

Additional reporting by Kris Bramwell & Bernadette McCague.

Business.title: Energy bills: What is happening to gas and electricity prices?
Business.text:
Energy bills are to soar in January, as prices governed by regulator Ofgem's cap rise at the coldest time of the year.

The cap affects millions of people in England, Scotland and Wales, and reflects higher wholesale gas costs which have been pushed up by the US-Israel war with Iran.

It means people on variable tariffs should give an accurate meter reading, ensure they are receiving all the support to which they are entitled, and take care over energy use.

The energy cap fixes the maximum amount which customers on standard variable tariffs can be charged for each unit of gas and electricity used.

It covers more than 20 million households in England, Wales and Scotland and is set by the regulator Ofgem every three months, external.

It affects those paying by direct debit, by standard credit (they pay when they get a bill), or prepayment meters in slightly different ways.

Most of the increase in the energy price cap has, and will be, driven by higher gas prices.

The government's decision to temporarily remove VAT from domestic electricity bills has cut about £45 a year from a typical bill.

Meanwhile, millions of households will receive a £100 automatic payment to help cover winter costs.

Customers' actual bills depend on the amount of energy they use and how they pay for it.

From January, for those on variable tariffs:

For electricity, average unit prices will go up on 1 January from 26.32p per kilowatt-hour to 32.69p

Gas will increase from 7.97p per kilowatt-hour to 10.96p, higher than in the wake of the invasion of Ukraine

Daily standing charges will be 54.77p for electricity and 29.65p for gas

The roughly 11 million households on fixed tariffs will not see their prices change until the end of their fixed term.

Ofgem regulates the energy market in England, Scotland and Wales. Northern Ireland has a separate system.

As well as how much energy you use and how you pay for it, where you live, the type of property you have, how energy efficient it is, how many people live there, and the weather all make a difference.

The Ofgem cap is illustrated using "typical" household energy use in a year with a single bill for gas and electricity settled by direct debit.

The vast majority of people pay their bill this way to help spread payments across the year.

In July, Ofgem reduced what it believes to be a "typical" level of energy use, because many homes have cut back due to high prices in recent years while energy efficiency has improved.

Its new estimate is 9,500 kWh of gas and 2,500 kWh of electricity a year.

Submitting a meter reading when the cap changes means you are not charged for estimated usage at the wrong rate.

This is especially important when prices go up.

Customers with working smart meters do not need to submit a reading as their bill is calculated automatically.

Ofgem also controls standing charges, which are a fixed daily fee to cover the costs of connecting households to gas and electricity supplies. These vary slightly by region, external and payment method.

Between 1 October and 31 December 2026, average standing charges for direct debit customers are 54.83p a day for electricity and 29.68p a day for gas.

From January, daily standing charges will be 54.77p for electricity and 29.65p for gas.

The electricity standing charge is lower than the amount charged over the previous three months, while the gas charge is largely unchanged.

Campaigners have long argued that standing charges are unfair because they make up a bigger proportion of the bill for low-energy households. Others say it just shifts the cost from one part of the bill to another rather than cutting it.

The government has announced plans to remove gas standing charges, although no details have been published on how that will happen

Fixed deals provide certainty for a set period – often a year, or longer – but if energy prices drop while you are on the deal, you could be stuck at a higher price.

You may also have to pay a penalty to leave a fixed deal early if you change your mind.

Experts recommend checking whole-of-market energy price comparison sites to help find the best deal and studying the details of exit fees.

Suppliers must offer customers affordable payment plans or repayment holidays if they are struggling to pay their bills. Most also offer hardship grants.

Since the Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022, bills have gone up by about 70% compared with the pre-crisis norm, and since then unpaid bills and charges have shot up.

Vanessa Northam, director at debt charity StepChange, has advice for people who may be struggling:

Take stock of all household money coming in and going out.

Look closely at how much energy you are using, and be alert to estimated bills, which might prove to be inaccurate.

Tell your supplier if you think you are going to struggle.

It is often best to try to talk to someone who can fully understand your situation.

Energy UK has a list of support schemes., external

Heating oil is not covered by the energy cap. About 1.5 million UK households use heating oil and they have already seen a sharp increase in bills since the Middle East conflict triggered a jump in oil prices. Some users have seen costs more than double.

The issue is particularly acute in Northern Ireland, where about 500,000 homes use heating all, almost two-thirds of all households.

In March, the government announced a £53m support package to help low-income households in rural communities who use heating oil.

Business.title: Nvidia value climbs by almost $1tn and tech stocks rally after Jensen Huang returns
Business.text:
Nvidia's market value rose by nearly $1 trillion as its share price skyrocketed after the tech firm reinstated Jensen Huang as its chief executive with immediate effect.

His shock reinstatement comes less than two weeks after Huang resigned after admitting an affair with a woman who was alleged to be a Chinese spy, a period in which shares in the chipmaker have also fallen significantly.

Nvidia shares rose by more than 31% which also lifted stock markets, with the tech-heavy Nasdaq climbing by 6.5% and the S&P 500 also rose 4.75%.

Tech stocks more broadly have also rallied following large falls on Friday, with much of the rally starting in pre-market trading before Huang's return was announced.

Other chipmakers experienced large increases following Monday's announcement from the Nvidia board. Shares in Micron Technology jumped 19%, while AMD shares rose nearly 7%.

Tesla shares also lept up by nearly 11.5%, while other tech gains were more muted by comparison: Amazon shares were up nearly 3.5%, and Apple and Microsoft rose by less than 2%.

While the surge in Nvidia shares was large and drove its market value back towards $4tn, the firm's share price remains about 21% down from a month ago.

A sharp drop occurred on 4 November, after the Democrat's midterm election victory sparked fears of tougher AI regulation to come led to a broad tech stock sell-off.

On Friday alone, Nvidia shares fell by 13.7% as tech stocks more broadly fell, and as Reuters reported - unconfirmed by the BBC - that the company was being investigated by the US Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) over its accounting practices.

Nvidia is a key firm at the core of the artificial intelligence (AI) boom, with the chips it makes central to the industry.

Nvidia's board of directors voted unanimously to reinstate the firm's co-founder following "a series of discussions and meetings" with him, the company said - but US President Donald Trump has claimed he "convinced" the board to reinstate Huang.

Kathleen Brooks, research director at brokerage firm XTB, said Huang's return showed Huang was the "godfather" of AI, and "has a talismanic influence over the sector".

"Barely two weeks ago this man was ousted from the company that he founded due to serious misconduct and potential national security issues," she said.

"Even though Huang did not hold special voting shares on the board, Nvidia's directors cannot see a future for the company without him."

Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell, said Huang's reinstatement was an astonishing about-turn for Nvidia, particularly given reports of an as-yet unconfirmed SEC investigation.

"This is the biggest corporate U-turn in living memory. To go from being embroiled in a spy scandal to being reinstated as the head of one of the world's most valuable companies in less than a fortnight is nothing short of remarkable," he said.

"Today's stock market rebound represents a massive sigh of relief by investors. However, one cannot rule out a more conservative approach by Huang going forward.

"His every move will be scrutinised by the market, and he may wish to tread more carefully to protect his integrity and ensure that Nvidia is being run responsibly."

Politicians are also demanding greater scrutiny.

Senator Jeanne Shaheen, the top Democrat on the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said Huang's reinstatement "reportedly at the encouragement of Trump Administration officials and without any apparent accounting or response to the risks to our national security, demands an explanation."

She added: "What is abundantly clear is that the AI industry requires guardrails and oversight."

Business.title: Judge blocks Brendan Carr-led FCC from taking any further action against ABC’s licenses
Business.text:
The federal judge Loren L AliKhan on Wednesday granted a preliminary injunction blocking the Brendan Carr-led Federal Communications Commission (FCC) from taking any action curbing ABC’s ability to renew its broadcast licenses, after the network sued the agency in August over an unusual demand to apply early to renew the eight local licenses for stations it owns.

The FCC claimed that the early renewal process was necessary to procure documents related to an ongoing Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (DEI) investigation, but the network countered that it was being punished for editorial coverage that was deemed critical of the Trump administration. The FCC’s order came after Donald Trump and the first lady, Melania Trump, criticized ABC for a comment made by the late night host Jimmy Kimmel.

At a hearing early last month, AliKhan seemed skeptical of the FCC’s reasoning for the early renewal order.

In her ruling, the judge said that ABC is “likely to succeed on their first amendment claim” of retaliation.

In addition to granting ABC’s request for a preliminary injunction, the judge denied the FCC’s request to dismiss the case. But she also denied ABC’s request to prevent the FCC from taking “any actions, formal or informal, to coerce or threaten plaintiffs with sanctions in an effort to alter their exercise of editorial discretion”.

In her ruling, the judge acknowledged the seriousness of the possible penalties facing ABC – and the chilling effect produced by an early license renewal order on a news organization’s first amendment rights. “Given the extreme, indeed existential, nature of the possible penalty Plaintiffs face – loss of their broadcast licenses – the court concludes that early license renewal proceedings create a risk sufficient to chill a broadcaster of ordinary firmness,” she wrote. “Any broadcaster of ordinary firmness – wealthy or not – would not hesitate to think twice if faced with such an existential threat to its business.”

The judge highlighted Trump’s long-standing animus against ABC as a clear factor in the FCC’s actions. “Starting with expressions of hostility, President Trump has set his sights on Plaintiff ABC for several years now,” she wrote, adding that the chairperson, Brendan Carr, “has taken President Trump’s rhetoric as his marching orders”.

As for the timing of the early renewal order request, coming soon after Trump’s criticism of Kimmel, the judge wrote: “Against the backdrop of President Trump and Chairman Carr’s call-and-response, it is no coincidence that President Trump criticized Mr. Kimmel’s skit on social media and the very next day Defendants initiated the early license renewal proceedings.”

The judge also noted the odd timing of the early renewal order, coming more than a year after the FCC began investigating ABC. And she acknowledged as credible the network’s concern that the agency’s license review process could run indefinitely.

“The existence of other mechanisms to solicit public input, coupled with the untenable timeline, casts serious doubt on the argument that Defendants are using the early license renewal proceedings to enhance public participation,” she wrote. “All told, the ‘significant mismatch’ between Defendants’ decision to order the proceedings when they did and their stated rationale for doing so presents an air of pretext the court will not ignore.”

In a statement, an ABC News spokesperson said: “Today’s decision is an important victory for the First Amendment. We thank the court for its careful consideration.”

Anna M Gomez, the lone FCC commissioner appointed by a Democratic president, also celebrated the judge’s ruling. “This decision shows that this FCC is a paper tiger whose threats crumble when challenged by those willing to defend their rights,” she said in a statement. “For nearly two years, the agency has weaponized its licensing authority to retaliate against broadcasters for exercising their right to free expression, and now a federal court has stepped in to put a check on that conduct. That brings badly needed accountability to a Commission and an administration that have politicized the machinery of government in a sustained campaign of censorship and control. Every broadcaster facing this pressure should take note and choose courage over capitulation because, as I’ve said from the beginning, the First Amendment is on their side.”

“While we appreciate the district court denying in part Disney’s request for preliminary injunctive relief, the portion of the decision granting Disney’s motion is wrong on the facts and wrong on the law – as controlling Supreme Court precedent makes clear,” a FCC spokesperson said in a statement. “The FCC looks forward to prevailing in full on this matter. We will continue to use our lawful authority to hold broadcasters accountable to their public interest obligations.”

Business.title: US inflation hits highest since May after prices climb 3.8% over the last year
Business.text:
The sell-off in US tech stocks continued on Wednesday as investors reacted to continued concern over the AI trade and fresh data that showed inflation jumped in October.

The tech-heavy Nasdaq index was down over 4% on Wednesday morning, while the S&P 500 had lost over 2.5% and the Dow had dropped about 2%. By the end of the day the tech-heavy index was down 0.6%, the S&P had lost 0.25% and the Dow managed a small gain of 0.33%.

After a rally upon the return of CEO Jensen Huang, Nvidia was down 5% at market’s closing on Tuesday and fell another 4% on Wednesday.

Anthropic shares rose 1% to end the day at $82.79, marginally lower than the $83-a-share price it was listed for during its blockbuster IPO last week.

New data released on Wednesday had shown consumer prices rose an annualized 3.8% in October, the highest rate since May.

This is the last inflation reading before a crucial US Federal Reserve board meeting next month, in which officials are largely expected to hike interest rates for the second time this year. The Fed has set a target inflation rate of 2%, a level not seen since February 2021. Higher interest rates make it more expensive to borrow money, slowing price increases, and raising the price of loans like mortgages and student debt.

Prices rose 0.3% from September to October amid soaring energy prices, according to the personal consumption expenditure index, the Fed’s preferred inflation measure from the commerce department’s Bureau of Economic Analysis.

The data comes after the Bureau of Labor Statistics separately reported prices climbed 0.4% from September to October, higher than economists had anticipated.

Energy prices, including gas prices at the pump, have cooled, going from a high of $4.41 a gallon in early October to $3.61 a gallon by mid-November, according to AAA.

Though Fed officials held rates steady at the last board meeting in late October, minutes from the meeting showed that some expressed concern about inflation’s stickiness.

“A few of them warned that further delay risked allowing high inflation to become entrenched or necessitating a larger and more disruptive tightening later,” the minutes said.

The move would come at a tumultuous time for the US economy. A new survey from the Conference Board released on Tuesday showed consumer confidence had ticked up in November to its highest level since January 2025, probably driven by the shake-up from the midterm elections.

Sports.title: Man Utd on wrong end of more controversial decisions in Sporting draw
Sports.text:
Two games, no wins. Two red cards, two goals scored. One goal disallowed, six conceded. Is it possible for Mauricio Pochettino to have learned anything from a crazy first week as Manchester United boss?

United and Pochettino went on the warpath before the Champions League encounter with Sporting, furious at Leny Yoro's dismissal at Liverpool which they believe was unjust and shaped the eventual 4-0 defeat.

Club officials were seething after the 2-2 draw in Lisbon as well.

This time it was 2022 World Cup final referee Szymon Marciniak in the firing line. Blowing before Amad's first-half header went into the net meant VAR had no chance to assess whether the Polish official was right to rule Youri Tielemans had fouled Goncalo Inacio before prodding the ball through to the Ivorian.

Former United winger Ashley Young didn't think so. He called Marciniak's performance "a disgrace".

That Tielemans picked up a booking that eventually led to his late red card – the Old Trafford outfit have now had four players sent off in their past five games, meaning the Belgian will miss the Old Trafford clash with RB Leipzig on 8 December - just compounded the situation.

Then, in a matter of minutes, Marciniak decided neither Manchester United keeper Senne Lammens nor Sporting counterpart Kaique had been fouled as they conceded. Their respective defences complained bitterly. Marciniak was only asked to go to the pitchside monitor by VAR for the latter incident, which he overturned.

United insiders felt the Tielemans incident was clearly not a foul and Amad's goal should have stood. They also felt any foul on Kaique by Patrick Dorgu was marginal and did not warrant their goal being disallowed.

Pochettino trod a fine path, knowing if he said something too controversial, it could land him with a fine.

A nod of a head in agreement was his initial reaction in his post-match news conference, when asked if he felt Marciniak had got it wrong.

A few minutes before, he was more expansive when he spoke to TNT.

"It's difficult to find a game where you get punished [so much] in one game," he said. "We were punished a lot in key actions."

Not for the first time this season, United controlled extended periods of a game they ended up not winning.

The goals they conceded at the Jose Alvalade were bizarre.

Seventy-five seconds after superbly saving one penalty, goalkeeper Lammens suffered a rush of blood and conceded another, which was scored.

Lammens was at fault for the second, when he dropped the ball into the path of Sporting striker Luis Suarez, who scored with an overhead kick.

"I think we dominated and we deserved to win the game, but we didn't for different circumstances," he said.

"All the teams make mistakes, but for these mistakes the punishment (for us) is too big in every single mistake. Many other clubs make mistakes or tilt in a different circumstance, in a more positive way. But that is in the way we are. We need to take responsibility."

United are still to win away from home in any competition this season. They have now won once in their last 13 matches. In the Champions League, they are 19th, two points in front of Roma, who are just below the top 24, which guarantees passage to the next phase.

Sports.title: 'All coming together' - Isak repaying Liverpool faith
Sports.text:
Liverpool fans have needed to be patient to see the best of Alexander Isak after an injury-hit start to his career, but the striker is now proving the wait has been worth it.

By scoring twice against Club Brugge in the Champions League, Isak took his tally for the season to 10 - more than double his total for his first season at the Reds.

Of course, that campaign was disrupted; he had no pre-season because of his protracted £125m move from Newcastle and then suffered a broken leg in December.

But Isak is now in a hot streak of form, having scored four goals in his past four games for Liverpool.

Asked whether fans were now seeing his full capabilities, Isak told TNT Sports: "It is always difficult to say exactly where you are and how good you are but I can definitely say I feel good, I am in a good place and the team is in a good place which is the most important thing.

"Hopefully it just gets better."

When Isak scored his opener against Club Brugge, it marked a sixth consecutive away game in which he has struck.

That meant he joined an exclusive club of just eight players to have achieved that feat, following in the footsteps of Dick Forshaw, Sam English, Gordon Hodgson, John Evans, John Aldridge, John Barnes and Mohamed Salah.

Isak has now scored the joint-most away goals across all competitions this season (eight – level with Erling Haaland).

His total is also already more than any Liverpool player managed away from home in the 2025-26 campaign (six by Cody Gakpo, Dominik Szoboszlai and Virgil van Dijk) and it is only November.

Isak looks to be brimming with confidence, exemplified by his second goal as he latched on to a pass from Alisson to go through one-on-one and then chipped a confident finish past the goalkeeper.

But for Andoni Iraola, Isak's performance offered much more than goals, the Liverpool manager also praising the striker's overall contribution.

"He is in a great moment right now," he said.

"In the first half especially he helped us with the link up. In the second half it was more about defending a little lower."

Former Liverpool defender Stephen Warnock agreed that Isak had shown he has more to his game than the goals.

"There were a lot of questions about Isak last year, about his price tag and what Liverpool paid for him," he said.

"There were a lot of people saying he doesn't take people on, but now he looks fitter and looks sharper and we are starting to see the quick, nimble feet again that we saw at Newcastle, with his nice touches and link-up play.

"So we are starting to see a different side of him. My big question in this system would be - can he press? Can he close down, can he affect the game in the other way that Iraola likes to do? Now we are starting to see that.

"All of it is coming together, which is great for him."

It is not just Isak who is looking the part in the Liverpool attack.

Florian Wirtz continued his impressive run of form with a goal that means he now has eight goal contributions in his last five games for Liverpool and Germany.

"Both are now in a good place," Iraola said of Wirtz and Isak.

"When the team overall is playing well and we are getting good results everything looks a little better.

"The important part if they help the team to play well and get results. Alex and Florian right now are in a good moment."

But the Liverpool attack as a whole is looking dangerous, regardless of who plays along with Isak and Wirtz.

In Wednesday's 3-0 win, it was Victor Munoz and Bradley Barcola who completed the front four, while in Sunday's 4-0 defeat of Manchester United it was Rio Ngumoha who played in Munoz's position.

"We have so many good players in our team," Wirtz told TNT Sports.

"Even when we can substitute some wingers, midfielders or strikers in the 60th minute or later it gives us a lot.

"It shows how good our team is and it is important for a top team to have a strong bench."

Liverpool's win against Club Brugge was their seventh from their last 10 games across all competitions.

"I spoke to Wirtz at the weekend, after the [Manchester] United game, and we were talking about his form - and he said 'well it helps that the team are playing well'," Warnock added.

"It's true because if you try to influence a bad team or a team that's not playing well, then it is much harder.

"With a fitter Isak, Wirtz looks a better player because now he is playing balls in behind that Isak is getting to, and getting in on goal on the back of.

"It has a knock-on effect, which is obviously like Wirtz said, he is playing in a team which is better equipped to suit him."

Sports.title: Aaron Rodgers: Pittsburgh Steelers release four-time MVP as starting quarterback
Sports.text:
Veteran quarterback Aaron Rodgers may have played his last game in the NFL after being released by the Pittsburgh Steelers.

In a brief statement published on Wednesday afternoon local time, the Steelers announced Rodgers, the NFL's four-time Most Valuable Player, was no longer with the franchise.

That came hours after Rodgers appeared on US sports TV programme the Pat McAfee Show and confirmed his time with the Steelers was over.

"That ship has sailed," he said.

Rodgers, who turns 43 next week, was also critical of Steelers head coach Mike McCarthy, including accusing him of snoring while he slept through team meetings.

Shortly before the Steelers confirmed his release, McCarthy responded to that interview, telling reporters "there was an ultimatum made that was clearly outside his job description", adding it was his decision to let the player go.

All this came after the Steelers had said on Tuesday that Mason Rudolph will be their starting quarterback for Friday's home game against the Denver Broncos.

The Steelers added that Rodgers would be inactive for the game, so would not serve as back-up to 31-year-old Rudolph.

McCarthy was in charge of the Green Bay Packers for most of Rodgers' 18-year spell in Wisconsin, including their Super Bowl win in 2011.

Rodgers, who joined Pittsburgh in 2025 after two years with the New York Jets, was "99% sure" he was going to retire after leading the Steelers to last season's play-offs.

However, McCarthy's appointment by Pittsburgh persuaded him to play one more year.

But Rodgers told the talk show on Wednesday the season had not been "what I signed up for".

Although the Steelers have a 6-4 record, they have suffered two straight defeats after losing 19-16 at the Philadelphia Eagles on Sunday.

When asked about a potential change on Monday, McCarthy said "Aaron Rodgers is our quarterback".

But a day later the Steelers announced that is no longer the case - and now they have gone a step further.

Pittsburgh's brief statement confirming Rodgers' release, external is likely the unceremonious end to an illustrious career.

While Rodgers was unable to claim a second Super Bowl win, he was named the season MVP in 2011, 2014, 2020 and 2021. Only Peyton Manning (five) has won the award more times.

Rodgers insisted his 22nd year in the NFL would be his last, and he has been let go at a crucial stage in the season.

The Cincinnati Bengals (7-3) lead the AFC North division, with Pittsburgh third, but with seven games left the Steelers occupy the final play-off spot for the AFC Conference.

Although Pittsburgh are 6-4, they have had to grind out some of those wins as they have struggled offensively. They rank 22nd for both points and passing yards per game.

Rodgers is undoubtedly past his best, but his form has only dropped slightly from last season and the team's struggles are by no means entirely down to him.

The Steelers' depth among their wide receivers is thin. Michael Pittman is out injured and DK Metcalf has not delivered the production expected when he was brought in with Rodgers before the 2025 season.

Metcalf, 28, was even ejected during Sunday's loss at Philadelphia, meaning Rodgers had to lean on debutant Max Hurleman with the game on the line.

And it is not as if Pittsburgh had a hot-shot rookie quarterback pushing for an opportunity to impress.

Rudolph is in his ninth season and has started each as a back-up. After being drafted by the Steelers in 2018, he joined Tennessee for the 2024 season then returned to Pittsburgh, starting 19 of his 38 career games.

McCarthy is hoping Rudolph can spark his offence, but if he doesn't, would they revert to the two young quarterbacks on their roster?

Teams seldom make such a sudden change at this stage in the season, especially those with a winning record and a quarterback of Rodgers' stature.

Rodgers has clashed with team management, team-mates and coaches throughout his career - including McCarthy - but the latest of those fallings out is certainly not the farewell one of the greatest quarterbacks of all time was hoping for.

Sports.title: Motorcycle catch: Man who caught a cricket ball on a moving vehicle found
Sports.text:
"I told my friend riding the motorcycle to duck his head. I'm going to catch it."

These are the words of Mehran Khan, who amazed sports fans around the world when he caught a cricket ball while sitting on the back of a moving motorcycle.

Mehran was passing a match in the Swat Premier League in Mingora when a ball sailed out of the ground towards him, with the passenger reaching out to catch it one-handed.

Speaking to the BBC, he said of the grab, which has gone viral online: "I didn't think I would actually catch it."

The employee of the Public Health Engineering Department was on his way home from work when he saw the ball being struck.

"I'm a cricket fan. I play cricket myself and I watch it too. I saw that Abrar Lala was at the crease and then he hit a six," he said.

"I told him [the friend who was driving] to duck his head. I'm going to catch it. Then I caught it.

"I made the effort, but I didn't expect to catch it. I thought it would fall somewhere nearby, but by the grace of God I managed to catch it."

According to Mehran, immediately after the catch the Swat Premier League organisers announced a prize of 10,000 Pakistani rupees (about £27.60) for him, funded by the Pakistan Army.

The Marghazar resident was caught by surprise when the recording of the catch spread so quickly online, saying: "The video went viral overnight. I didn't even know about it."

He expressed his happiness at receiving the award, saying he was grateful to God, and added that he had returned the ball after taking the catch.

"People are saying I was taking the ball away with me, but that's not true. I returned it," he said.

Swat Strikers won the match against GKR Dir by 34 runs, and Mehran urged the organisers to continue holding the tournament every year, describing it as an "excellent competition".

Sports.title: Raheem Sterling: After court case how common is nitrous oxide in football?
Sports.text:
It is known as laughing gas but the impact nitrous oxide can have on a professional footballer's body is anything but funny.

"I'm not going to name names but I have colleagues who know Premier League footballers who are no longer playing as a direct result of nitrous oxide [use]," said Dr David Nicholl.

Nicholl, a clinical lead in neurology with Sandwell and West Birmingham NHS Trust, was speaking after former Manchester City, Chelsea, Liverpool and England forward Raheem Sterling was handed a suspended jail term after pleading guilty to dangerous driving.

A key part of the case was that Sterling had been inhaling nitrous oxide from a balloon while driving.

His Lamborghini was seen veering across a motorway and later crashed into a metal gate. Sterling, 31, was arrested at the scene and found with six gas canisters in his car.

He disclosed to custody staff "he had a problem with nitrous oxide", the court was told.

Defending Sterling, Jason Bartfeld KC said his client "recognised the various unhealthy coping mechanisms that brought him to this position" and that he has "sought to address" these in the "most positive and effective way and with some success".

So, what is nitrous oxide, how does it affect those who take it and is its use more common in footballers than the wider population?

Nitrous oxide's original use was as a sedative that healthcare providers like dentists could use to keep patients comfortable during procedures.

It is now legally sold for catering, medical and industrial purposes, but is frequently used as a recreational drug and is commonly known as laughing gas.

This can be abused by inhaling the gas via a balloon, leading to a short-term high causing symptoms such as brief euphoria, mild perceptual changes and uncontrollable laughter, external.

Nitrous oxide also slows brain and body responses and can displace oxygen in the lungs and bloodstream, contributing to dizziness, confusion or fainting.

It is thought long-term or excessive use can have disastrous effects on the body, from neurological harms to nerve and spinal cord damage which could lead to permanent disability.

According to medical journal The Lancet, it is now the third most commonly used drug after cannabis and cocaine in the UK, with use highest among people aged 16–24 years.

It has been increasing in popularity as a recreational drug over the past decade.

This prompted it to be reclassified as a Class C drug in 2023 after a government consultation.

BBC Sport has been told the abuse of so-called laughing gas has been widespread among professional footballers for a long time.

Former player Drewe Broughton is now a human performance coach, working with Premier League footballers and clubs around the world.

He said laughing gas was seen by some as a release.

"I think the use of nitrous oxide is really common," he added.

"It's something that can be done in private. It's something that can be hidden. You can't smell it on their clothes or the breath. It's an underground thing."

Broughton said he had been in the company of professional players when they had been using 'balloons'.

"I remember sitting in a players' house on the outskirts of Manchester, and these canisters were all over the floor," he added.

"I was from a world where people drank or they gambled or went to pubs and nightclubs. That was my first exposure to it."

Broughton has developed an app to help tackle issues with mental health and under-performance in football.

He said the reasons to use nitrous oxide had always been there: pressure on players to perform leaves them searching for an escape.

But Broughton has concerns about the toll nitrous oxide can take.

"I don't think there's the same awareness around nitrous oxide and damage to the body as there would be around alcohol or other drugs," he said.

BBC Sport has been told that some footballers see laughing gas as an alternative to harder substances because it does not stay in the body's system for more than a few hours.

Luci Hanmer, who works with Lancashire drugs and alcohol support charity 'We Are With You', said a substance like nitrous oxide was hard to detect.

She said: "Anything that you're inhaling, the effects that you're going to feel happen very soon.

"So if you are looking for that escapism, the effects are going to be quick.

"Once ingested, it doesn't last very long within your body compared to some of the other substances which can be detected for quite a number of days.

"So if you're getting a drugs test the next day for example, that won't show up."

Former Manchester City defender Nedum Onuoha said more support was needed, particularly for players like Sterling who break through young.

Sterling made his debut for Liverpool and England at just 17 - before going on to win four Premier League titles at Manchester City and 82 caps for his country, including the Euro 2020 final at Wembley.

"Look at what's happened to Raheem," he said. "Look at how this led to this moment, a moment which I'm sure he's hugely embarrassed about, because I'm sure he can see how dangerous that was to not just his life, but the lives of so many people who are on the road at the same time.

"But I just don't feel like football is in a position where they think it's important to support people who have issues with nitrous oxide."

The BBC Radio 5 live pundit said the use of nitrous oxide in professional footballing circles was very common.

"I think the difference from when I was younger is that people would openly party in certain places," he said.

"Now they party where they're harder to spot. That's why you don't really see on a week-to-week basis now the scandal of somebody that's been out drinking.

"The players are doing it, but it's more sophisticated in terms of how they do it, the locations, and this is an example here with nitrous oxide."

Neurologist Dr Nicholl has been working with patients who have abused nitrous oxide for years and issued a warning to others.

"It certainly is being used by footballers, but it's pretty much the worst thing that you want to be using if you're a professional sportsperson," he said.

"It damages your spinal cord and the spinal cord is a bit like an electrical cable, where the insulation - the outside of that cable - gets stripped away.

"So what patients will complain of is difficulty with feeling on their hands or feet, or unable to walk at all.

"So, in effect, it's like a spinal cord injury. But they can also get blood clots, deep vein thrombosis, pulmonary emboli, and some patients have died."

If you have been affected by any of the issues raised in this story, information and support can be found at the BBC's Action Line website.

Sports.title: 'Disgrace' decisions, divots and howlers - Man Utd chaos against Sporting
Sports.text:
Manchester United were held to a draw in a chaotic and controversial Champions League encounter with Sporting in Lisbon with Mauricio Pochettino denied a first win as United head coach despite his side turning around a first-half deficit.

They were behind at the break after goalkeeper Senne Lammens conceded from a penalty he gave away – having saved another just minutes before.

United then had a goal disallowed before scoring a penalty of their own through Bruno Fernandes, who then put them in front with the help of a large divot on the pitch.

There was more drama as Lammens dropped the ball for Sporting's equaliser before Pochettino's side had what they thought was a winner ruled out.

Polish referee Szymon Marciniak was at the centre of much of the drama with midfielder Youri Tielemans sent off in stoppage time.

BBC Sport breaks down each incident after a crazy night.

Lammens went from hero to zero in the space of 76 seconds as he rushed out of his goal and took out Maxi Araujo in the United box.

Noussair Mazraoui was caught out by a ball over the top but it was reckless from Lammens and this time Suarez buried the spot-kick.

Former United midfielder Owen Hargreaves told TNT Sports: "There is no way Senne Lammens can get there. Just stay in the goal."

Amad Diallo thought he had equalised for United before half-time when he headed in after his first attempted was turned on to the cross bar.

However, referee Marciniak blew his whistle for a foul against Youri Tielemans.

Replays showed Tielemans won the ball and pulled out of the challenge after he played the ball through to Amad.

BBC Sport's Dale Johnson: "Marciniak believed that Goncalo Inacio had been fouled by Youri Tielemens on the edge of the area as the Manchester United midfielder played a pass through.

"Rather than immediately blow his whistle, Marciniak held off to let the move play out.

"But when Diallo hit the bar with his first effort, Marciniak blew his whistle.

"Play was dead at that point, so when Diallo then nodded the rebound over the line the VAR was locked out.

"However, the chances that the VAR would have intervened were very slim.

"Tielemens, who was booked, caught Inacio's foot under his body sliding to make the pass, causing the Sporting defender's ankle to buckle."

Former Manchester United midfielder Ashley Young said on BBC Radio 5 Live: "It's an absolute disgrace. I don't know how the referee is seeing that Tielemans has kicked the player.

"On first viewing, I thought his foot must have hit him on the follow through but when you look at it again, Tielemans actually tries to take his foot away.

"He doesn't touch him because he knows the midfielder is coming towards him.

"It is one of the worst decisions I've seen with a referee giving that decision."

United took the lead with two quick-fire goals but in bizarre circumstances as Fernandes' speculative strike looked like it would be easily collected by Kaique Pereira only to hit a divot on the pitch and fly up past the Sporting goalkeeper.

Former Rangers striker Ally McCoist on TNT Sports: "I think it hits a divot and it jumps over the goalkeeper! That is absolutely incredible."

Hargreaves added on TNT Sports: "Unbelievable. It is like a golf divot. There are holes in this pitch absolutely everywhere.

"Bruno Fernandes created a divot, does he get an assist for that?"

Midfielder Tielemans was then sent off for a late challenge on Sergi Altimira. The Belgium international's second yellow compounds the controversial one he received in the first half.

United have now received five red cards in all competitions this season - two more than any other Premier League side.

Young added: "The referee's performance was just simply 'wow'.

"The decisions that he gave. Youri Tielemans getting booked to eventually getting sent off later because you booked him when it should never have been a booking and it should have been an equalising goal.

"His decision-making today is nothing more than a disgrace."

Sports.title: Manchester City: Football regulator chief 'has stomach' to take action against club
Sports.text:
The chair of English football's independent regulator has told MPs he "has the stomach" to take potential action against Manchester City.

The club was found guilty of breaching Premier League financial rules over a nine-season period by an independent commission.

The verdict, published in September, found City's Abu Dhabi owners - a private investment company belonging to United Arab Emirates vice-president Sheikh Mansour - inflated revenues and disguised losses by £900 million through "sham" arrangements.

City deny wronging and have appealed, but if the ruling is upheld, they could face an investigation by the Independent Football Regulator (IFR).

It has the power to remove directors if they are deemed unsuitable, and even to force a sale of the club.

Appearing in front of parliament's Digital, Culture, Media and Sport select committee, IFR chairman David Kogan was clear that the watchdog would not be afraid to investigate the club's hierarchy and take action, if deemed necessary.

"Forget the name of the club, forget the size of the club, forget the scale of the issue. We cannot simply ignore our statutory duties in relation to a club because it happens to be of a certain size," he said.

"We absolutely will have to take the appropriate action as laid out in the legislation, depending on the circumstances as they come to us, which are the evidence that's been presented and collated by the independent commission of the Premier League and by any judgement that takes place on that evidence through an appeal.

"But in one sense, the evidence has already been judged by those cases having been found guilty, so we will absolutely have the stomach to do so.

"Would I, with an organisation that has a relatively new, fairly young staff, that's been going for less than a year, would I have chosen to have this particular issue in our laps this early? Well, probably not.

"But the truth is, if we don't act - assuming those circumstances are triggered - if we don't act, what is the purpose of having a football regulator?

"So I think we have to absolutely, clearly be seen to be doing the job that you as legislators have asked us to do, and we absolutely will do that, whatever that means."

The fallout from the case has prompted concern that wider UAE investment in UK projects could suffer. In September, Prime Minister Andy Burnham was criticised for saying he would be "really concerned" if the scandal led to City's owners selling the club.

Kogan added: "Does the evidence, if we come to assess it in relation to individuals, stand up in terms of the legislation as being a cause for concern? And if it is, we will have to act appropriately.

"That is the only test, not the politics around it, not the place where it came from, not the size of the club. It is the only test because without that, you cannot have an effective regulator."

When asked how any possible legal battles with City would be paid for, IFR chief executive Richard Monks said a litigation reserve of £2m was to be built up over the next two years via a levy charged to the clubs. "When we take litigation, we expect to win and we expect to reclaim costs and repay that reserve from costs," he said.

"Now clearly - and I'm not talking about a specific case - clearly, there could be a very large legal case of any particular club that would require us to spend more than £2m in terms of litigation costs and barrister costs in particular. So if that happens, we have agreed with government [that it] will effectively lend us the money in terms of cash flow.

"As I say, we'd expect to win that litigation, to claim costs and repay government. If we failed in that massive litigation, then ultimately it would be added to the levy and we'd repay government that way."

Sports.title: The Hundred to introduce semi-finals from 2027
Sports.text:
An extra match will be added to The Hundred for the first time in 2027 with the introduction of semi-finals.

In the previous six editions of The Hundred, only the top three qualified from the eight-team group stage. First place went straight to the final, with second and third playing in the eliminator.

Now, the top four will play in traditional semis in a move designed to increase the competitiveness of the group stage and create an extra marquee fixture.

The Hundred window will not be expanded to accommodate the semi-finals – the competition will still be completed in just under four weeks.

Instead, finals weekend will be altered. In 2026, for the first time, a reserve day was scheduled for the eliminator, which was played on a Friday before the final took place on a Sunday.

In 2027, the semi-finals will take place on Friday and Saturday, followed by the Sunday final.

The Oval has become the regular venue for the eliminator, with Lord's hosting the final. Having both games in London has minimised travel for the teams having to play an extra game to reach the final.

In the new structure, The Oval is expected to host the Saturday semi-final. The venue for the first semi is to be confirmed.

The tweak in the format of The Hundred comes a year after investors began to exert influence over the eight franchises.

In 2025, the England and Wales Cricket Board sold stakes in all eight franchises, raising more than £500m to be distributed across the game. Investors became involved in the running of their teams ahead of the 2026 season.

The move to introduce a second semi-final has not been directly influenced by the arrival of external investment, though it has been welcomed by owners.

A primary motivation has come from a desire to maximise the competitiveness of matches played in the latter stage of the group phase.

The Hundred group stage is relatively short – only eight matches per team – meaning the margin between qualifying or missing out on the play-offs can be thin.

In the 2026 men's competition, fourth-placed MI London finished on the same points as Sunrisers Leeds in third. On the women's side, Manchester Super Giants finished fourth, two points behind Southern Brave, yet Super Giants were one of only two teams to have a match abandoned because of the weather.

The 2027 Hundred is set to begin on 3 August, the day after the scheduled fifth day of the final Ashes Test between England and Australia at The Oval. The Hundred finals day will be held on 29 August.

Trent Rockets are the defending women's champions, while Manchester Super Giants are holders of the men's title.

Sports.title: EA adds AI-generated John Motson to FC 27 video game
Sports.text:
Football game EA Sports FC will feature the digitally recreated voice of the late commentator John Motson, Electronic Arts has exclusively told the BBC.

Motson, who died in 2023, was the main commentator for BBC Sport for decades - and performed the same role for the video game series during the 90s and 00s.

It is the first time the hit series, formerly known as Fifa, has featured a deceased commentator.

With the permission of his widow and his son, Motson's voice has been synthesised using a combination of old recording sessions and generative AI. It will become available in FC 27 on 26 November.

The legendary commentator died aged 77 in February 2023 - several months after the launch of ChatGPT and the massive growth of AI it set in train.

Fred Motson told the BBC it "means an awful lot" to have his dad's voice in EA Sports FC once again.

"I grew up with Fifa," he said. "I always used to tell my parents that I needed the latest console for Christmas because otherwise dad couldn't see how the game worked."

Electronic Arts, which was bought for $55bn (£42bn) in August, told the BBC it paid Motson's family for the rights to use his likeness and recreate his voice, but would not disclose the financial terms of the deal.

The BBC's lead football commentator Guy Mowbray said it was a "privilege" to be involved in the game, which he has provided commentary for since 2023.

"I think it's quite a nice, sort of non-scary use of AI," he said.

"We're in the business of nostalgia... I hear commentary not in my own voice, but in John's voice, because that's the voice I knew growing up.

"So I think it's nice that that legacy can be continued in this way."

John Motson was the first commentator for the series, appearing on games from Fifa 96 up to Fifa 2005. He later made a brief cameo in Fifa 19.

"While he completely understood when they went in a different direction, I think he really missed it after he left the game and it felt like a bit of an end of an era," his son said.

EA told the BBC the studio would not have included Motson in the game unless they had permission from his family.

"There was no way we would have moved forward with this in any way, shape or form if they weren't fully on board," said Mat Prior, senior game design director at EA Sports FC.

"At the outset we wanted to pay tribute to to Motty as the commentator and as this emotional connection - he was the very first voice of our game - so we really wanted to do him justice and bring him back."

He explained that Motson's voice in the game was a combination of old lines he recorded over the years and AI - tech which he said was "the only way" to make it happen, as they don't have recordings of him talking about modern players like Bradley Barcola and Chloe Kelly.

Motson's son Fred said he believed his dad would have "absolutely" wanted to be involved in the game after his death.

"My dad was the least technological person in the world," he said. "Till his dying day, he had a typewriter on his desk.

"So I don't think he would have quite understood what the AI was doing technologically - but I think, on the other hand, he was always really keen to get involved in these kinds of projects."

But Peter Caulfield, founder of Save Our Voices Now which campaigns against AI voice cloning, expressed some disquiet about the project, and the fact Motson had been unable to consent to it.

"If someone has signed a deal allowing their likeness to be used after they die, I have no issue with that," he said.

"But in life or in death, unless you have specifically agreed to it, AI cloning of any kind should not be allowed.

"Being a family member shouldn't automatically give you that right either."

Sports.title: Steelers release Aaron Rodgers after he accuses Mike McCarthy of sleeping during meetings
Sports.text:
The Pittsburgh Steelers released Aaron Rodgers on Wednesday, hours after the four-time NFL MVP accused head coach Mike McCarthy of falling asleep during team meetings.

Rodgers made the sensational allegations during a surprise 34-minute appearance on ESPN’s The Pat McAfee Show after the Steelers benched him in favor of backup quarterback Mason Rudolph.

“We have released QB Aaron Rodgers,” the Steelers wrote on X. If no other team claim Rodgers on waivers, he will become an unrestricted free agent. Several teams, including the Indianapolis Colts and New England Patriots, are in need of a starting quarterback at the moment.

McCarthy, who was also Rodgers’ coach with the Green Bay Packers, had said on Monday that the 42-year-old was still the team’s starter despite recent struggles. On Tuesday night, the Steelers changed course and said Rodgers, one of the greatest players in NFL history, would be deactivated for Friday’s game against the Denver Broncos.

During the interview, Rodgers said his time with the Steelers was over. “That ship has sailed,” he said. He then described a quarterback meeting the previous week.

“Last Wednesday, we were in a quarterback meeting. Mike came in late, sat down, and within 10 minutes began snoring. Woke himself up, was rattling his papers,” Rodgers said. “We all looked around. Five minutes later, you hear the snoring again. And less than five minutes after that, he walks out of the room like nothing happened.”

Rodgers added that he only found out about McCarthy’s decision when his teammate Pat Freiermuth told him. Rodgers said Freiermuth had called him and said “I can’t believe they’re doing this.” To which Rodgers replied: “Doing what?”

Rodgers, who said this summer that he would retire at the end of the season, also alleged that McCarthy appeared to think he was still coaching the Packers during Sunday’s defeat to the Philadelphia Eagles. “The nail in the coffin for so many of us was at halftime, towards the end of it, we’re kind of on the offense on one side of defense on the other side,” said Rodgers. “And there’s some rambling or something [from McCarthy] and without even a heads up, he says, ‘All right, one, two, three Packers.’ That’s what he broke it down on in the locker room … [We] looked around going, ‘What the fuck? What is going on? Where’s his head at at this point?’” ESPN reported that multiple sources agreed with Rodgers’ version of events.

Rodgers said he had spoken regularly to McCarthy over the last few days, and the coach had not mentioned the possibility of being benched. He did, however, say they had discussed McCarthy sleeping during meetings. “[I told McCarthy], we can’t even have an honest conversation. I’m telling you, you snored in the meeting twice, in a quarterback meeting, that’s unacceptable,” Rodgers said. “And you’re telling me you’ve never slept at a facility before. And I’m telling you, I have a hundred witnesses and collaborating people who would support what I’m saying. I’m not saying that to fucking bury you.

“I’m saying that because this behavior and these habits are not healthy and they’re not becoming of someone intimately involved in the game plan. And that’s my whole point. And so, I left it with him that if you try and bench me or don’t change the play call, then you should just release me because I feel like at this point, I’m doing what’s right for the organization”. Rodgers said after his comments to McCarthy that the coach decided he was “getting rid of me”.

The Steelers (6-4) have lost their last two games but are still clinging on to the final playoff place in the AFC. NFL Next Gen Stats gives them a 62% chance of making the postseason, although the model does not take into account players flambéing their own team’s coach on live television.

Rodgers is considered one of the greatest quarterbacks of all time, someone whose single Super Bowl win does not match his natural talent. He is all but guaranteed to be a first-ballot Hall of Famer. His NFL records include highest passer rating for a quarterback with a minimum of 1,500 attempts (102.5), highest passer rating in a single season (122.5 in 2011) and lowest interception rate in a season (0.3% in 2018).

Gaming_Tech.title: Trump's accounts traded Nvidia shares 44 times this year, records show
Gaming_Tech.text:
Donald Trump's investment portfolios have bought or sold shares in chipmaker Nvidia at least 44 times this year, a review of the US president's financial disclosures shows.

Trump's most recent public declarations of his investment trading show that between January and September the portfolios purchased between $5.2m and $17m (£4m and £13m) in Nvidia stock - and sold between $4.4m and $12m. His portfolios held between $12.5m and $58m of Nvidia shares at the end of 2025.

Financial disclosures to the Office of Government Ethics report a low and high range of transaction values, so a more precise analysis of how much Nvidia stock was traded is not possible.

The period of recent turmoil at Nvidia and volatility in its share price is not covered by the disclosures. In the last two weeks, co-founder and chief executive Jensen Huang resigned and then Trump played a significant part in his reinstatement.

The White House has said that Trump's stock and bond portfolio is independently managed by third parties and neither he nor his family "has any ability to direct, influence or provide input regarding how the portfolio is invested or when investments are bought or sold".

Huang resigned on 12 November after reports of extramarital affairs, including with one woman who has alleged ties to Chinese intelligence. Nvidia's share price dived following news of his resignation.

But on Monday Nvidia's board announced the 63-year-old was being reinstated as CEO.

Trump told US media he had "made the deal" to "convince" the tech giant's board to bring Huang back. The board said it had "received input from senior levels of the United States government" that he posed "no national security risk".

Nvidia's share price surged 31% on Monday following Huang's return. About $1tn (£763bn) was added to Nvidia's market value, but the company's shares are still trading below their value before reports of Huang's alleged affairs began to circulate.

However, concerns remain among both Republican and Democratic politicians about Huang's actions and Nvidia's compliance with US controls over the export of advanced computer chips to China, as well as Trump's involvement in getting him reappointed as CEO.

Gaming_Tech.title: Huawei found guilty of stealing US trade secrets but acquitted of racketeering
Gaming_Tech.text:
Huawei has been found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets and bank fraud, but not guilty of the more serious overarching racketeering charge in a landmark case in the US.

In a two-month trial, prosecutors accused the Chinese technology and telecommunications giant of lying, cheating and stealing to gain any competitive advantage.

Huawei's defence team argued that prosecutors had decided Huawei was a criminal organisation and built its case from there, but the firm's success was due to its own innovation.

Huawei said, external the racketeering acquittal "confirms that these allegations lack factual basis", adding that it would "take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests".

Jurors in a Brooklyn court found Huawei guilty of 10 out of 12 counts, which included conspiracy to violate US sanctions.

However, the jury declined to convict Huawei of the racketeering conspiracy charge, which required members to find the firm acted like a criminal enterprise.

Federal prosecutors first announced the charges against Huawei in 2019, after the dramatic arrest in late 2018 of senior executive Meng Wanzhou in Canada.

Meng, also known as Cathy Meng, was held for three years in Canada before she was released to return to China through a deal with US prosecutors.

During closing arguments last week, assistant US attorney Meredith Arfa told jurors Huawei spent 20 years doing whatever it took to expand its business, including lying to banks about its business dealings in Iran and stealing technology secrets from rival firms to ensure it had a competitive edge.

"For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft," US Attorney General Todd Blanche said in statement, external.

"Thanks to the work of the FBI and our federal prosecutors, those who engaged in these criminal activities will be held accountable."

The Chinese government hit out at what it called the US "suppression" of Chinese companies and said it supports Chinese firms protecting their interests.

Defence attorney Brian Heberlig said it was by dint of hard work that Huawei's business had expanded with operations in 170 countries and more than 200,000 staff.

Following the verdict, Heberlig told the BBC that Huawei was gratified that the jury had rejected the racketeering charge.

"The RICO [Racketeer Influenced and Corrupt Organizations Act] count that alleged that Huawei was a corrupt organisation, with a corporate culture and policy of committing crime. That was, in our view, a significant overreach, and the jury soundly rejected it," he said.

"Of course, we have mixed emotions about the rest of the verdict ... [we] thought that Huawei was deserving of acquittals across the board."

Sentencing is planned for September 2027. Heberlig said there will be "significant advocacy" to achieve the lowest sentence possible. Following that, he said he fully expects Huawei to appeal.

"If I know Huawei, that fight will continue, and the company's not going to rest until it's pursued every last argument it can through appeal, and hopefully, ultimately toward vindication," he said.

Gaming_Tech.title: Zoe Kleinman: Nobody is irreplaceable - unless you're Jensen Huang
Gaming_Tech.text:
Remember the tech boss and his head of HR, both married to other people, who were caught on camera at a Coldplay concert with their arms wrapped around each other?

Their horrified reaction went viral, and the pair both resigned. Astronomer, the firm where they both worked, said their actions had fallen short of its standards.

Compared with the scandal which has engulfed Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang in recent weeks, that Coldplay kiss cam moment now feels rather tame.

Huang admitted to having had an affair, reportedly with a woman accused of being a Chinese spy.

There were suggestions that she may have been involved in smuggling Nvidia chips into China, in breach of a US export ban.

Concerns about national security had reached the desk of US President Donald Trump.

There were other stories about some of Huang's relationships with female colleagues.

For most of us, that would without question amount to instant, and irreversible, dismissal.

But while Huang briefly left the company, he was just as swiftly reinstated, and welcomed back with open arms.

As I watched footage of him being greeted with cheers, applause, high fives and a big hug back at the company's HQ on Monday, I wondered how many disgraced bosses would kill to be in his shoes.

"Imagine being that Coldplay CEO reading all the comments on here about how it's OK if you're actually a good enough CEO," quipped menswear writer Derek Guy on X, external.

Huang has blown out of the water the old adage that nobody is irreplaceable.

Despite names of potential permanent replacements being bandied around, Nvidia's board evidently reached the same conclusion - interim chief executive Colette Kress was in for less than two weeks.

So how on Earth did he manage it?

Well firstly, Huang is the boss of a company that has manoeuvred itself into a uniquely powerful position.

Nvidia's computer chips are considered the best in the business for driving AI.

Demand for its latest tech is through the roof and the firm sets its prices accordingly: Its Rubin and Vera GPUs sell for tens of thousands of dollars each, and one data centre might contain hundreds of them.

So, the US AI sector relies on Nvidia, Trump is determined that the American AI industry needs to be the best in the world, and Huang is the only leader the company has ever known.

He's been at the helm for 33 years and he's a computer scientist himself, renowned for being very hands-on with the development process. (Whether the boss's input is always wanted is another matter, but it's always there.)

Working for Huang isn't easy.

Long hours are normal and negative feedback is often given in front of everyone else.

When he wants something to happen, he doesn't stop until it does: one of his early ideas was to halve the chip production cycle, in order to get one step ahead of the competition with their longer lead times for orders.

Lots of experts told him it couldn't be done. Until eventually, they did it.

Not only does Huang have technical expertise, he's also a charismatic figurehead, representing Nvidia at events around the world in his trademark leather jacket, rubbing shoulders with world leaders, royalty, and fellow tech bosses.

For many, he's become something of a cult figure. Nvidia sometimes sells limited edition clothing at conference pop up stalls. A jumper featuring a cartoon image of Huang costs $178 (£137).
