Entertainment.title: Reeling in the years: how Hollywood fell for its own vanishing glories
Entertainment.text:
If Los Angeles was a person, it might just be a laid-back fiftysomething trouper with cool sunglasses and an even better haircut. Some dodgy episodes in his past, but still handles himself with style. In other words, Los Angeles personified is Cliff Booth – the over-the-hill stuntman played by Brad Pitt in Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood, now turned studio fixer in the sequel, The Further Mis-Adventures of Cliff Booth.

Set eight years later in 1977, Further Mis-Adventures is more plot-driven, more Elmore Leonard-esque than the pure expansive “memory piece” of Once Upon a Time. But both films are steeped in the ambience and lore of old LA, drawn in part from Quentin Tarantino’s memories of cruising around the streets aged six in his stepdad’s Karmann Ghia (the car Booth also drives). They’re part of the recent intensely nostalgic LA revivalist mini-boom of work that also includes Paul Thomas Anderson’s Licorice Pizza (2021), Damien Chazelle’s Babylon (2022) and Ti West’s MaXXXine (2024).

It’s no accident that this retrospective crew is in high gear just as Los Angeles, and Hollywood, hit the skids in real life. Runaway production to other states and overseas has been sapping the heartland of the California film industry for decades: from its peak in 1996, feature film activity in the city had dropped by 50% by 2013 – and has further declined since. The cardiac arrest suffered by theatrical box office during Covid and the post-2022 streaming slowdown pushed it deeper into the red zone: 42,000 jobs have been lost over the last two years. With half-empty studio lots, landmark talking shops like Patrick’s Roadhouse dying out and swathes of iconic neighbourhoods ravaged by wildfires, the current fear is that job-stealing AI will further hollow out the city, inducing an irreversible state of digital dereliction.

No wonder returning to the 60s and 70s to soak up the agent chat at the bar at Musso & Frank, or bask in Sharon Tate basking in her own image at the Bruin theater, is comforting. The late middle-aged LA revivalists like Tarantino, David Fincher (who’s taken over directing from Tarantino on Further Mis-Adventures) and Anderson (who also made the similarly LA-besotted Inherent Vice in 2014) were too young to have experienced that era directly. But hitting working age in the 1990s, the final generation to experience Hollywood’s pre-digital imperial phase, they are the ones now memorialising its heyday as a creative powerhouse.

Like today’s AI inflection point, many of the LA revivalist films deal with a moment of transition. Once Upon a Time is caught between the tail end of the stodgy studio system represented by Leonardo DiCaprio’s floundering star Rick Dalton and the New Hollywood noisy neighbours of Roman Polanski and his ilk. And like today’s furore over AI slop supplanting human-led film-making, a strain of panic runs through the new films about the survival of true cinema. “You know what we gotta do? We gotta redefine the form,” says Pitt, playing a silent-film veteran staring down the barrel of the talkies in Babylon. “The man who puts gasoline in your tank goes to the movies – why? Because he feels less alone there. Don’t we owe him more than the same old shit?” Mia Goth’s porn star Maxine Minx, hoping to cross over to “real” movies in 1985 LA, is on the receiving end of a similar pep talk from her director in MaXXXine.

So staring into the abyss of the San Andreas fault and fearing for its soul is nothing new for Hollywood. Often for the current revivalist crew, it’s an elusive woman who crystallises this search for a halcyon authenticity: “This is the girl”, as David Lynch intuited a long time back in Mulholland Drive. In Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood, Sharon Tate is the golden-tressed spirit of aspiring LA – and actor Margot Robbie repeated a similar job with her wild-child ingenue in Babylon (with a near-identical scene of watching herself in the cinema). Inherent Vice isn’t specifically about the film industry, but the disappeared Shasta Fay Hepworth leaves behind an incense whiff of the lost idealism of hippy California. Seemingly hunted by serial killer the Night Stalker, Maxine Minx looks destined to become another LA sacrificial woman – until she bucks the trend and saves herself.

But finding “the girl” – or in other words sifting the real from the fake – is no cinch in Los Angeles, the town that made its name intertwining the two. Trudging in the footsteps of Philip Marlowe, Inherent Vice and David Robert Mitchell’s Under the Silver Lake (2018) both feature pseudo-detectives trying to decode this city of signifiers. Also hanging on a missing girl, the latter film stages its own inquest on Angeleno artistic integrity: its arch-conspiracy leads to a mysterious songwriter who devastates Andrew Garfield’s slacker by telling him he manufactured all his favourite rebel alt.culture.

It’s Tarantino, though, who supplies the subtlest take on the twin spooling of representation and reality in Los Angeles. Already Pulp Fiction – the movie he has deemed closest in spirit to Once Upon a Time … in Hollywood – took place at a retro-tinted remove from the actual city. But his 2019 masterpiece lingered in backlots and dressing rooms, making full use of its backstage pass to tease out the interplay of artifice and life in a series of paradoxes. It’s Cliff Booth, the behind-the-scenes stalwart, who supplies the film’s movie-star moment when he walks tall into the Manson family’s Spahn Ranch. Meanwhile, screen star Rick Dalton gets a lower-key, realistic triumph: besting his insecurities and alcoholism to finally deliver “the best acting I’ve ever seen in my whole life”. And in rescuing Sharon Tate from her grisly real-life fate, Tarantino delivers the ultimate movie resurrection.

But perhaps, pained by an industry on the brink, the new pack of sentimentalist LA redeemers wilfully misremember their history. Perhaps the reality is there was no Hollywood golden age, no well of authenticity. Fabrication and artifice are the city’s true trades. Tarantino also knows this, as the irony about movie-star facades – Bruce Lee included – in Once Upon a Time lets on. Paul Thomas Anderson is even clearer about this tawdry fabulation factory in Licorice Pizza, with its San Fernando valley milieu of cocky teen actors, Sean Penn’s leathery star vaingloriously recreating a stunt outside the Tail O’ the Cock restaurant on Ventura Boulevard, and an explosive cameo for legendary hairdresser turned cokehead producer Jon Peters. The most truthful scene in the otherwise coarse and forced Babylon is the one-shot through the multitude of entertainments shooting out on the desert lot: the radical, illusionistic inauthenticity of Hollywood production in full flow. As Cliff Booth has it in Mis-Adventures: “I know better than to get in the way of a good story.”

The least bewitched film about the city is Thom Andersen’s 2003 cine-essay Los Angeles Plays Itself, which is clear-eyed about its penchant for constant self-erasure and reinvention. In this sprawling “any city”, there is no there there – least of all in Hollywood. This floating constellation of studios and production companies is a fungible entity. He points out that Culver City in 1937 almost renamed itself Hollywood, trying to grab some of the glory. Even the sign itself – which, unlike film-industry self-obsession, Andersen tolerates – is testimony to this incorrigible restlessness: “Maybe I find it poignant that a decayed advertisement for a real-estate development could become a civic landmark.”

With AI knocking, Los Angeles and Hollywood are about to head somewhere else. Likely the industry will absorb and integrate the technology, and emerge leaner and meaner, a little more cynical, a little less interesting. Some people will have to find new lines of work. Like Cliff Booth, you could do worse than becoming a fixer. There’s never a shortage of work, because Hollywood, and Los Angeles, can’t be fixed.

BreakingNewsTab.title: German boat dealer suspected of supplying Channel smuggling gangs, BBC finds
BreakingNewsTab.text:
A German boat dealer is suspected by European authorities of being a key supplier to migrant smugglers operating in the English Channel, the BBC can reveal.

Nearly a third of small-boat crossings in the first four months of this year allegedly involved boats or engines from MaReBoote, a small firm in western Germany, according to files we have seen.

The managing director, Marvin Reuter, is contesting extradition to France, where he could face smuggling, criminal conspiracy and involuntary manslaughter charges.

His equipment is suspected of being linked to two fatal accidents, in which four men died.

We confronted the 35-year-old at his business near Dortmund, but he would not answer our questions. He said he was reporting us to the police.

Reuter cannot be formally charged until extradited to France but could face jail time, if tried and convicted. He is presumed innocent until proven guilty.

The BBC - alongside German broadcasters WDR and NDR, newspaper Süddeutsche Zeitung (SZ) - and France's Le Monde newspaper - has obtained and reviewed hundreds of police, court and tax documents about the case. We have blurred images of Reuter because of German privacy rules.

Investigators, we have learned, believe they have uncovered clear, persistent links between Reuter and smuggling networks.

Evidence has been gathered through the confessions of alleged accomplices and covert jail-cell recordings of an alleged gang chief - as well as the two deadly crossing attempts.

At least 82 boats from Reuter's firm reached the English coast in just over two years to May, according to French investigations.

There are also press photos dating back five years showing the MaReBoote logo on dinghies crowded with migrants.

In 2021, Reuter told the Sun and Guardian he felt "frustrated" and "anxious" that his vessels had ended up in the hands of smugglers.

There was no suggestion, at that time, that authorities suspected him of wrongdoing as a German detective reportedly told the Sun: "This would be like if somebody buys a Mercedes and does something in another country which is wrong. The Mercedes seller can't help that."

It is not exactly clear when police suspicions were aroused.

French prosecutor Samuel Finielz would not comment on the details of the investigation but confirmed the head of a German company is currently the subject of a European Arrest Warrant.

The warrant was issued in May this year and relates to alleged offences dating back to December 2024.

While selling boats is "perfectly legal" it becomes illegal, said Finielz, "when one is fully aware that they will be used by networks involved in illegal immigration or human trafficking".

Case files we have seen say that German police had learned from UK authorities that 29% of detected crossings this year, up to the end of April, involved boats and/or engines linked to MaReBoote.

In France, five other men have already been charged as part of the investigation - an Iranian, three Iraqis and a Syrian.

In one of the two fatal incidents where Reuter's equipment is suspected to be involved, one of those who died was also Syrian.

Suliman al Husein would have just turned 20 when he died, according to a birth date listed in the files.

News reports at the time say he suffered a cardiac arrest after likely being crushed on a packed dinghy during a failed launch, west of Calais, in January 2025.

He was the first migrant to die in the English Channel that year. His body was found on the floor of the boat which, investigators allege, bore the MaReBoote logo.

The case against Reuter also stems from a chance arrest when French police pulled over a vehicle with German plates, near the northern port city of Boulogne-sur-Mer.

The BMW, which was towing a trailer, was spotted overtaking another vehicle at speed in the early hours of a morning in May this year - police records say.

Inside the car were two German nationals who - according to a subsequent search - were transporting jerry cans of fuel, a boat engine, pumps and a rolled up inflatable dinghy.

The men claimed they had been paid up to €1,000-a-time (£830) to make several, similar drops to "foreigners" on the coast, interrogation records show.

"Of course I knew that it wasn't legal," one is said to have admitted under questioning. "The money made me turn a blind eye."

Take a look at BBC Verify's UK migration tracker - the latest numbers on net migration, visas, asylum and small boats

Both men, who have since been convicted for smuggling offences, allegedly implicated Marvin Reuter as the man who had hired and paid them for this work.

Police files say both the BMW and the boat it was carrying had MaReBoote logos on them.

Marvin Reuter was arrested in Germany in May and later released, pending extradition.

On the day of his arrest, German police also seized more than 30 dinghies and 9,000 life jackets. Equipment which, we can now reveal, was allegedly linked to Reuter.

The BBC was previously granted access to see this haul, held in a police warehouse at a secret location in western Germany.

In Germany, it became explicitly illegal to aid smuggling to the UK at the end of last year after a prior BBC investigation exposed the country's role as a storage hub for gangs. Before then, some anti-smuggling laws in Germany had no longer applied to the UK because of Brexit.

The raid that saw the seizure of equipment that was allegedly linked to Reuter marked the first time the new law had been used.

Small boat crossings have dropped significantly in 2026, with British authorities citing law enforcement as a "key factor". However, illegal migration into Europe has also been falling.

The UK National Crime Agency's (NCA) deputy director for organized immigration crime, Dan Cannatella-Barcroft, praised Germany's "commitment" to tackling people-smuggling but acknowledged the country would remain "an important piece of the puzzle".

While a gap in the law has been closed, Germany's proximity to France, wider transport links and the fact that some of the Kurdish-dominated gangs are based there, means it is expected to stay as a transit point in the illegal small-boats trade.

The "vast majority" of small boats equipment in the past few years has come through Germany, Cannatella-Barcroft told the BBC - much of it made in China and having been routed through Turkey.

BreakingNewsTab.title: New UK-EU treaties have 10-year termination clause, BBC understands
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The government and the EU are set to publish the texts of two treaties that were agreed last week as part of a post-Brexit reset.

The treaties will be published on Thursday afternoon, alongside legislation which is designed to enact the bulk of the deal.

The BBC understands the treaties have a 10-year termination clause that would mean if one party ended the agreement, they would have to pay to rebuild border checks infrastructure, which will be significantly scaled back as part of the new deal.

Opposition leader Kemi Badenoch and Reform UK's Nigel Farage have suggested they would refuse to pay.

The Brexit reset deal has already sparked debate about its benefits, its costs, and a wider discussion on the long-term UK-EU relationship.

The deal covers British food exports, emissions trading and a youth experience scheme.

Two of the three legal texts will be released on Thursday, covering the food trade and emissions trading scheme deals, alongside the government's cost-cutting bill to enact the deal.

New assessments of the impact of the deal on different sectors and regions of the country are also expected.

Under the deal, food exporters will be significant beneficiaries from the scrapping of considerable red tape and checks, and dismantling of border facilities. An internal analysis forecasts a 16% boost to agricultural exports.

The industry and government hope the reduction in costs for food producers and sellers will be passed on to customers, but there may be no clear visible impact at the checkout.

Privately, industry insiders told the BBC earlier this week that there are too many moving parts in the world economy, in particular the energy price shock resulting from war in the Middle East.

Regarding the fine detail in the text of one of the treaties relating to the 10-year termination clause, European affairs minister Hamish Falconer said: "The Cutting Costs Bill allows us to implement two major trade agreements."

"It allows us to eliminate paperwork for our food and drink traders, protect billions of pounds worth of British exports from carbon taxes, and make doing business with our largest trading partner cheaper and easier."

The BBC understands that a plan to link British and European emissions trading schemes will see more coverage across the UK's aviation and maritime industries.

The treaty text will also contain finer detail of how the UK will observe, shape but not vote on relevant EU rules.

Plans to use secondary legislation, including granting direct so-called "Henry VIII powers" to ministers to align UK and EU laws, will also be detailed in the legislation.

Such powers could enable ministers to make changes to bills with less Parliamentary scrutiny.

Outlining the agreement with the EU to MPs earlier this week, the prime minister said new agreements with the EU are "pragmatic" and "not a prelude to anything".

Andy Burnham also said it would be "unthinkable" for the UK to rejoin the bloc without a referendum.

Several former prime ministers have urged him not to reopen the Brexit debate. Burnham said they are "stuck in the past" and later claimed there would be "no banging on about Europe" from Labour.

Badenoch said Burnham has "oversold" the deal and was "trying to take Britain back to 2015".

BreakingNewsTab.title: Expect fewer frosts and more hot days as UK seasons shift, says Met Office
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The UK's seasons are changing, with fewer winter frosts and more hot summer days, according to new analysis from the Met Office.

Across the UK, the number of winter days with an air frost – when the air temperature falls to 0C or below – was around a quarter lower in the decade to 2025 than during the period from 1961 to 1990.

In southern England, the reduction was around a third while the average number of UK summer days reaching 25C has more than doubled.

The Met Office says climate change has led to these seasonal shifts.

"Our summer is getting wider and our winter is getting smaller," says Dr James Pope, climate scientist at the Met Office.

"The driver of this is that the whole global climate is warming. And that impacts on the UK.

"Some areas went from their wettest ever winter to a severe drought via a record-breaking summer for the whole country."

The changing conditions have affected wildlife and led some farmers to grow different crops.

Some of the biggest reductions in winter air frosts have been in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, where the average number of days has fallen by around 11 compared with 1961 to 1990.

Southern England has seen other significant changes. In Cornwall, the average number of winter air frost days has almost halved, falling from around 18 to just 10.

On the Isle of Wight, the figure has also fallen by almost half, from around 21 to 11 days.

Scotland remains the frostiest UK nation, but has also seen a reduction, from around 45 to 38 winter air frost days.

The Met Office defines a hot day as one where the temperature reaches 30C or above.

Across the UK, the average number of these days has increased fourfold, from 0.3 to 1.2 per summer.

The increase is particularly striking in Greater London, where days reaching 30C have risen from an average of 1.3 to 6.1 per summer.

Summer 2026 was the hottest on record, according to provisional Met Office data.

There were five widespread heatwaves and 40 days of temperatures above 30C, smashing the previous record of 34 days.

"Humans, animals and crops are encountering extremes of temperature that we've not seen before and this is a physiological challenge to all three," says Thomas Crocker, science manager with the Met Office's climate security team.

This has led to water challenges, he says, with wet winters causing problems with planting, pests and diseases.

Dry summers have meant there has not been enough water to grow crops.

"The impact on horticulture is seismic, it's affected all crops," says John Walgate, CEO of British Growers, which represents most British horticultural organisations growing vegetable and fruit.

Walgate says this year's weather has been particularly tough for brassicas like cauliflowers, cabbages and broccoli, with yields down by about 50%.

Irrigated crops such as onions, potatoes and carrots also suffered from a lack of water due to low rainfall and hot temperatures.

It's not all been bad though. Walgate says soft fruit such as strawberries have had a "good year".

Tim Young and his family have been farming in Norfolk since the 1960s.

But his arable crops - onions, wheat and sugar beet - have been struggling because of the hotter, drier summers and fewer cold days in winter which kill bugs.

With some crop yields decreasing, Young has been looking at ways to diversify the farm's income and planted a vineyard three years ago.

Last year he harvested double the expected amount of grapes.

"With climate change, the frontier is moving further north of where we can grow grapes," he says.

Despite annual variations in weather, he is confident it can be profitable.

Changing weather patterns are shifting where species live and when they migrate, breed and feed, says Zoe Quiroz Cullen, head of climate and international policy at The Wildlife Trusts charity.

Warmer winters mean bats are waking from hibernation when there are too few insects to feed, she says, while amphibians emerging and spawning earlier can be caught out by cold snaps.

Meanwhile, warmer springs mean oak trees are coming into leaf earlier than usual, and caterpillars are hatching earlier.

The UK's bird population has fallen in recent decades, largely because of habitat loss and climate change, external.

Starlings and swifts have declined significantly, although milder winters and conservation work have helped some species thrive.

Kevin Anderson, visitor experience officer at Somerset Wildlife Trust, has worked at Avalon Marshes for 15 years and has seen its bird life change first-hand.

Thirty to 40 years ago, he says, it would have been rare to see an egret north of the Mediterranean.

Now the reserve is home to a growing population of great white egrets taking advantage of warmer winters which allow them to fish all year round.

The birds first bred in Somerset in 2012, with just two nests. Last year, about 73 chicks were born in Avalon Marshes with the population thought to be around 200 now.

Climate change - mainly the result of the burning of fossil fuels - is raising average temperatures in the UK.

The current global warming level is 1.4C above pre-industrial levels, climate scientists estimate.

The Met Office says changes to the UK's seasons are expected to continue as temperatures rise.

If global warming reaches 2C above pre-industrial levels, the UK could experience an average of about 24 winter air frost days, compared with 38 during the period from 1961 to 1990.

Summers could also become hotter.

The average number of days reaching 25C could rise to around 15 per summer, compared with just over four during the earlier period.

Crocker says the UK's weather in the coming years is going to vary.

"There's still going to be some cooler summers, there's still going to be some drier winters - but that baseline has shifted."

He says we will see more extreme hot weather and more record-breaking hot days, but we are less likely to experience extreme cold weather.

And Met Office research shows summer extending into autumn, and the possibility of less autumn rainfall in the future.

But Dr Pope says there will always be four distinct seasons in the UK.

The analysis has been done by the Met Office as it begins a new partnership with the BBC to provide weather data for weather forecasts, as well as additional insight and expertise on our changing climate.

BreakingNewsTab.title: BBC launches partnership with Met Office for weather coverage
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The BBC has said it will offer more regional, digital and 10-day weather forecasts under a new partnership with the Met Office, which begins on Thursday.

The collaboration, announced last year, aims to bring together the Met Office's weather and climate intelligence with the BBC's journalism and reach, the broadcaster said.

Director general Matt Brittin said the partnership would mean "serving our audiences with the most accurate, reliable and helpful weather service we can".

But the launch comes during a savings drive at the corporation, which has seen some other weather services and bulletins dropped as part of wider cuts.

The new Met Office partnership is unrelated to the cuts and was announced last July, before the BBC embarked on its latest round of savings.

The BBC said the partnership includes:

A new hourly forecast on the BBC News website and app covering 10 days, with improved medium-range forecasts

Met Office severe weather warning notifications via the BBC Weather app

More local and more digital weather reports, and more forecasts fronted by local weather presenters

More "content collaboration on BBC and Met Office channels" using Met Office expertise, and helping to explain weather and climate

There will also be Met Office branding on weather reports, and a new BBC weather centre based in the agency's headquarters in Exeter.

Brittin said the collaboration would involve "turning science into stories and helping audiences make informed decisions with our forecasts".

Met Office chief executive Penny Endersby said: "Today is a landmark moment as the Met Office and the BBC join forces to give even more people across the UK access to Met Office's accurate and trusted weather information."

She added: "Our new partnership with the BBC combines the Met Office's world-leading science with the BBC's incredible reach, giving a powerful opportunity to bring the story of our changing weather and climate to millions more people."

A previous partnership between the BBC and the Met Office ended in 2018.

Since 2018, the BBC's data for its weather forecasts has been provided by the Dutch MeteoGroup, which was later acquired by US weather services company DTN.

Separately, the BBC has dropped or shortened a number of national television and radio weather bulletins in recent weeks, as the corporation continues to work towards a £500m savings target.

Some weekend and late-night forecasts have been dropped from the TV schedules, with regional presenters instead now delivering a UK-wide weather outlook during their presenting slots.

Listeners have also complained about programmes such as Radio 4's PM no longer delivering a full weather bulletin, with presenter Evan Davis instead reading a short summary and directing listeners to the BBC website for a more detailed forecast.

The BBC said it was changing its weather team to better serve digital platforms, in line with audience research and changing consumption habits.

The corporation said more users are accessing weather information via the BBC's app, website and social platforms, as the number of people relying on broadcast bulletins declines.

A spokesman for the corporation said: "The BBC is committed to providing a world-class public service for weather forecasting and information across our platforms.

"As we announced in July, we are making changes to the way we deliver weather information as more people are turning to mobile and the website for their weather forecasts. We also recognise that people want more local forecasts, along with the national picture, to help them plan their coming days more accurately.

"As such we are providing more digital and localised forecasts, as well as ensuring we still have appropriate national weather bulletins across the TV and radio."

BBC Radio 4's Today programme, BBC Breakfast and the weekday editions of BBC One's News at Six will retain their usual national weather forecasts.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Stalking law simplified to become one offence
BreakingNewsTab.text:
A new standalone offence of stalking is to be created in England and Wales after a review found the law regarding the crime was "cluttered and confused" - but the maximum sentence will not be increased.

Specific stalking offences were introduced in 2012 but the underlying offence of harassment had to be established, and additional factors such as fear or distress proven, for it to be considered stalking.

A review was ordered by the government last year, led by Richard Wright KC, who prosecuted the man who stalked and murdered Alice Ruggles in Gateshead in 2016.

Victims of stalking have welcomed the change in law but said they were disappointed not all the recommendations have been adopted.

Katherine, from Newcastle, whose former partner was arrested 28 times for stalking her, welcomed the government's decision to introduce one stalking offence instead of two.

"I'm pleased about that one because my ex was charged with [the lesser offence] of stalking without fear to start with and I was terrified," she said.

"Anyone who's been stalked knows how terrifying it is, so that one [without fear] was just pointless."

But her ex had resumed his behaviour after being sentenced to three years and four months in prison, and she criticised the length of jail terms given to stalkers, which she described as "an absolute joke and an insult to the victims".

Ashley, from Washington, in Tyne and Wear, was also disappointed the maximum sentence would not be increased.

"Stalking can have a devastating and lifelong impact on victims and their families," she said.

"It affects your confidence, independence and ability to feel safe, even long after the relationship has ended and the perpetrator has been sentenced."

Of the two current offences, only the more serious charge, which requires proof of fear of violence on at least two occasions, can be tried in the Crown Court, where the potential sentence is greater.

The government has accepted the introduction of a single offence for stalking that can be tried in either Crown or magistrates' court and described it as the "biggest shake-up of stalking laws in more than a decade".

But documents seen by the BBC show ministers rejected Wright's proposal to raise the maximum sentence from 10 to 14 years.

Ministers said the average sentence for the more serious stalking offence in the year to March was 18.6 months, suggesting the existing maximum was not being fully used.

Safeguarding minister Satvir Kaur said: "It's really important that victims know that we are holding perpetrators to account and feeling the full force of the law.

"The average sentences being given aren't good enough."

She said judges were already able to jail stalkers for 10 years so it was better to work with them to make sure they used the powers available to them than "changing the goal posts" on the maximum sentence.

The review was submitted to ministers earlier this year and last month Alice Ruggles's father, Clive Ruggles, said victims of stalking would be at greater risk of dying if the government failed to publish and act on the recommendations.

Alice was killed in her Gateshead flat by her ex-boyfriend Trimaan Dhillon, who was found guilty of murdering the 24-year-old and jailed for 22 years.

Her family has campaigned for better recognition of stalking and improvements in how it is tackled.

Reacting to Thursday's announcement, Alice's parents said they "welcomed" the report and recommendations.

They added they were "heartened" that the response "endorses the need for a single stalking offence that focuses on the perpetrator's behaviour and removes the onus on police and the CPS to prove the impact upon the victim".

Wright's review concluded confusion between stalking and harassment laws could contribute to failures in identifying and prosecuting the crime.

A previous investigation into police handling of stalking found three in every 20 stalking crimes examined had been incorrectly recorded as other offences, including harassment.

The review also recommends removing the need for victims to demonstrate actual fear or serious disruption to their lives for a stalking offence to be established.

Wright argues this would better protect victims who were unaware they are being secretly followed or monitored.

The government said it would explore introducing such a test but had not yet committed to its inclusion in the new offence, although Kaur said she was "sick and tired of it being the onus on the victim".

The review called for more consistent police investigations and greater use of specialist interventions to protect victims.

It also raised concerns about stalkers using applications to change protective orders as a means of maintaining contact with, or control over, victims.

Wright suggests additional safeguards, including requiring court permission before certain applications can proceed and ensuring victims can make representations.

The government acknowledged the problem but said it needed to explore the suggestions further.

Ashley, who was stalked by her former husband Jason Howe using an AirTag to track her movements, said she was "genuinely disappointed" by this response.

Howe was jailed for three years and four months in March last year for stalking and controlling or coercive behaviour.

But Ashley later discovered a restraining order designed to protect her had been amended, without her being consulted, allowing him to use a road through an exclusion zone near her home.

"A restraining order is supposed to protect victims, not provide another opportunity for perpetrators to maintain control," she said.

The government has decided not to adopt a recommendation that would allow previously convicted stalkers to face a new stalking prosecution after just one further incident involving the same victim.

Instead, in previously announced legislation which comes into force on Thursday, courts will now be able to use stalking protection orders in cases of both conviction or acquittal.

"These orders can be in place for as long as is needed," Kaur said.

The government said it would introduce the new legislation as soon as parliamentary time allowed, but had not set a date.

BreakingNewsTab.title: US approves SpaceX plan to send a million data satellites to space
BreakingNewsTab.text:
US regulators have given SpaceX the go-ahead to launch a million satellites into Earth's orbit to help build data centres in space - the first approval of its kind.

The company, which is owned by Elon Musk, wants to use sunlight to power satellites that will process data for AI and send the results back to Earth.

The Federal Communications Commission (FCC) said on Wednesday that the project, known as Starmind, will "support America's booming super intelligence economy".

Its approval comes as communities across the US have pushed back against the expansion of data centres on the ground.

Space X believes the "orbital data centres" are the most cost and energy-efficient way to meet the growing demand for artificial intelligence (AI) computing power that is beyond "terrestrial capabilities".

FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement that the project "opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America's leadership and growth".

"This is the kind of American ingenuity that can unite our strengths in space and advanced technology, reinforce our economic leadership, and expand prosperity here at home," Carr said.

Responding to the announcement, Musk wrote on X: "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."

Under the FCC licence, deployment of the satellites has to begin no later than November 2033. SpaceX will be required to have deployed 10% by November 2035, rising to 50% by November 2038.

The company has already said it wants to launch its first Starmind satellite next year.

Its unclear if a million satellites will be launched or if SpaceX has sought approval for a higher number than it will use.

Like SpaceX's current Starlink network, which provides high-speed internet via more than 10,000 satellites, Starmind's satellites will operate in low-Earth orbit at altitudes ranging between 500-2,000km (310-1,242 miles).

Starmind's satellites will communicate with Starlink's and then relay the data to Earth.

The solar-powered satellite system "promises to bring the human race closer to a Kardashev II civilisation—one that can harness the full power of the sun", the FCC statement said, in a reference to a hypothetical society, proposed by an astronomer in the 1960s, capable of harnessing the entire energy output of its home star.

The orbiting data centre concept is also being explored by other firms - including Google and Blue Origin - and is being pitched as a greener alternative to traditional centres, which require enormous amounts of power to run and water for cooling.

The ever-expanding use of AI computing has seen a massive increase in the amount of data that needs to be stored and processed around the world.

New facilities continue to be built but it is becoming difficult to find places to put them. Data centres are large and sprawling, use enormous amounts of power and water for cooling, and increasingly local people don't want them built nearby.

Data centres were a central issue in the midterm elections earlier in November, with many Democratic candidates promising tougher regulation on their construction.

An expert previously told the BBC that launching hardware into orbit remains expensive and that the infrastructure to protect, cool and power them can be complex - while a growing quantity of space debris puts the physical hardware at risk.

Separately, another cautioned that the growing number of low-orbit craft increases the possibility of crashes between objects - which could damage machines or send materials falling back to earth.

Starlink has been accused of creating congestion in space, something Musk denies. He has also rejected claims his satellites have been taking up too much room and crowding out competitors.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Thirty-one killed in massive fire as fuel tanker crashes on Cairo highway
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Thirty-one people have been killed and 21 others injured in a large fire on a busy highway in Cairo after a fuel tanker crashed, Egypt's health ministry says.

Hospitals nearby treated patients suffering burns and smoke inhalation after the incident, which occurred on a section of a ring road in the Warraq neighbourhood, to the north of the old city centre, on Wednesday evening.

Footage circulating on social media showed billowing flames and black smoke towering high into the night sky, with multiple nearby vehicles torched.

Officials have not given an account of how the fire broke out, but state-owned media reported the tanker had overturned, dousing nearby vehicles with petrol.

The regional public prosecutor has launched an investigation into the incident and asked that DNA samples be taken from bodies of the dead.

The tanker, which belonged to a private contractor, had been travelling along the highway when a high-voltage cable fell in front of it, prompting the driver to lose control, Al-Ahram reports, citing sources with knowledge of the investigation.

It then crossed the central reservation, overturned and caught fire, the state-owned newspaper says.

Egypt has suffered several deadly fires in recent years, with informal residential areas and often run-down infrastructure making incidents more common, the response to which is often complicated by slow emergency response times and locally improvised rescue efforts, even in the sprawling Egyptian capital.

Images from the scene show a large crowd gathered on the highway after the fire had been extinguished, as emergency services blocked off entry routes.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Desperate appeals from women on death row in Iran after protests
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Taraneh Rahimi is on death row in Iran.

In recent weeks, the 21-year-old has been unable to walk properly after her legs were beaten, and an ear-infection caused by an untreated head injury has affected her balance, her cousin says.

She is "keeping her spirits up" but "there are days she breaks down in tears," Masoud Nourmohammadi tells BBC News Persian.

He says Taraneh and her twin sister Romina were arrested after joining the anti-government protests that swept the country in January.

When the twins' mother first saw them in prison, their faces were so swollen and bruised, and their hair pulled out, that she could only recognise them by their voices, Nourmohammadi says, speaking from the US.

He says Taraneh signed a confession after interrogators threatened that her sister would be raped in front of her.

Taraneh is one of six women who have been sentenced to death this year in connection with the January protests, according to the UN's human rights rapporteur for Iran, Mai Sato.

The figure for men is much higher. However, women protesters and dissidents are being sentenced to death in numbers not seen for decades, as part of a "horrific rise" in politically motivated executions, Amnesty International's Iran researcher Raha Bahreini says.

The Iranian embassy in London told the BBC that claims of an increase in the use of the death penalty in protest-related cases were "misleading".

It categorically rejected allegations of the use of torture and any allegations that the death penalty has been imposed solely for peaceful protest, which it said is a "legitimate, and protected right".

It said death sentences in relation to the "riot in January 2026" were issued in cases involving "intentional murder" or "Moharebeh (the taking up of weapons with the intent to threaten or wreck the people's lives or property)".

The twins were seized in late January, Nourmohammadi says.

It was two weeks after the end of the protests, which began in late December over economic grievances and grew to become Iran's largest against the clerical establishment since the 1979 Islamic Revolution.

The US-based Human Rights Activists News Agency (Hrana) says it has identified more than 7,000 people killed in the crackdown that followed, most of them protesters, but believes the true figure is much higher.

The Iranian government accuses the US and Israel of fomenting the unrest, blaming "terrorists" and "rioters" for the deaths, which it says totalled 3,117 including some members of the security forces.

The twins' family did not find out where they were being held for more than three months, their cousin says. They were tried over protests in Isfahan, in an area of the city where a member of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) security force was killed.

Court documents have not been published, but the BBC has seen part of a sentencing document which says Taraneh was convicted of moharebeh, which is a capital offence under Iran's Islamic Penal Code. The offence included "drawing a bladed weapon with the intent to endanger people's lives", according to the document.

Romina was sentenced to 25 years in jail for the lesser charge of aiding and abetting moharebeh, according to Sato, the UN rapporteur.

Nourmohammadi, who has been in contact with relatives and others in Iran familiar with the case, says both women deny all the charges against them and that there is no evidence Taraneh had a "bladed weapon".

Sato says the sisters were part of a case in which 10 people were sentenced to death, but that there was "no clarification of the acts attributed to each individual".

According to sources familiar with the case, the twins' lawyers have submitted a complaint alleging they were tortured and sexually abused during interrogation, but the investigation into it is being overseen by an official they accuse of torture.

Voice messages from other women on death row contain a mixture of desperation and defiance.

Mahboubeh Shabani - widely reported to be 33 and a civil engineer - was sentenced to death in September under Iran's espionage law after transporting injured protesters, according to rights groups.

She called for help for herself and other prisoners from jail in the city of Mashhad in north-eastern Iran: "Everyone is in a terrible place mentally, especially those whose sentences have been finalised," she said.

Also jailed in Mashhad is Najmeh Amini, reported to be 23, who was initially arrested in the wake of the January protests, and later sentenced to death after being convicted of committing blasphemy in a social media post, according to rights groups.

"As long as I am alive, I have one hope, and that is to see a free and prosperous Iran before my life ends by the noose," a voice message attributed to her says.

In addition, Mojdeh Hashemi Bazargani - reported to be aged 27 - is also facing execution, according to rights groups. They say she was convicted of charges including "espionage", after being arrested in April, during the current war between Iran and Israel and the US.

The US-based Iranian rights group Tavaana has shared audio it says is of a phone call she made from prison, describing being beaten in the head, neck and body and made to sign a confession.

The woman in the recording says: "They accused me of espionage. They say you've been paid for it. If I had been paid for espionage, I would have a car or a house. I have nothing."

Amnesty International describes the charges in all three of these cases and also the twins as "politically motivated".

In response to the BBC's questions, the Iranian Embassy in London said "any allegations of the use of torture in connection with the mentioned cases are categorically rejected". It did not comment further on individual cases, but said "confessions obtained under duress have no legal validity".

At least 39 people have already been executed in connection with the January protests, according to Sato.

She notes a "sharp" increase in arrests and sentences across both men and women, and sees the rise in death sentences for women as an "escalation and expansion" of an "established pattern of repression".

Iranian human rights lawyer Musa Barzin, who is based in Turkey, says "it appears that factors such as gender or age now carry less weight in determining the severity of punishment".

Official detail on cases is often scant and some may go unreported.

However, Sato says as well as the six women she identified as being arrested in connection with protests, a further three have received death sentences this year - for "blasphemy" and "corruption on Earth charges, in relation to the war in March" and "espionage and moharebeh".

In comparison, these nine sentences are more than Hrana recorded for women for similar offences over the whole decade to 2025 - with no more than three in any one year.

The death sentences in three of the cases Sato identified as being linked to the protests have since been overturned – though two of those have been sent for retrial. She says she is concerned by an "increasingly frequent pattern" where overturned death sentences are later "reimposed by a parallel branch of the judiciary once public attention has subsided".

Sato says there was a "turning point" for women in Iran during the 2022 protests over the death of Mahsa Amini, who died in custody after being detained over an alleged breach of Iran's dress code.

Women "were at the forefront of challenging state policies and structures of control," says Sato. "Their political agency, visibility and leadership have made them targets of state repression."

The Iranian embassy said judicial proceedings in Iran are conducted in accordance with the Constitution and rule of law. It adds: "Cases involving the death penalty have included charges such as serious criminal offences, violence, terrorism, espionage, cooperation with hostile intelligence services and Moharebeh."

Iran executes more people per head of population than any other country, according to UN experts. Human rights groups say last year saw the highest number in decades.

Hrana recorded 2,003 executions in the year to October 2026. The vast majority - including 47 women - were for crimes such as murder and drug trafficking.

Nourmohammadi says the family are trying as best they can to support the twins.

Romina enjoys music and often asks relatives to play songs over the phone, he says.

Taraneh loves horses and has always wanted to set up a horse breeding centre, he says, and they tell her they plan to help her do so in the future: "That's how we try to give her hope."

BreakingNewsTab.title: Government set to double spending on social media unit to £25m
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The budget for a government communications team which uses social media ads and influencers to reach the public has almost doubled since Labour came to power.

The New Media Unit, set up in 2024, is set to spend £25m this year on promoting government policies on YouTube, TikTok and other platforms, a Freedom of Information request by the BBC has revealed.

It comes as Andy Burnham was forced to defend his use of social media influencers to engage with young people, after a row over a video with explicit language that was recorded on the steps of 10 Downing Street.

The PM said the video was "not acceptable" and the creator of it, Max Balegde, had apologised and taken it down.

Burnham rejected calls from Conservative leader Kemi Badenoch to apologise for "debasing his office" and defended his strategy of appearing in influencer videos, arguing that was where young people got their information.

Balegde, whose real name is Max Trobe, was among about 60 content creators invited to Downing Street for a reception earlier this month.

The New Media Unit was not involved in the event on 9 November - but it has helped organise previous Downing Street receptions for content creators.

The FOI request reveals its budget has grown significantly in the two years since the unit was founded under Sir Keir Starmer, from £13.2m last year, to £25m this year.

It shows the unit's headcount has doubled too, from 21 employees last October to 43 today, as the government speeds up the shift towards digital communications.

The government says using digital platforms like TikTok, YouTube and Instagram is "the most cost-effective and direct way to reach many citizens, particularly harder-to-reach and vulnerable groups" who do not use traditional print, radio and TV outlets.

Most of this spending has been earmarked for "paid campaigns" online, with more than £8.8m spent since April.

Paid campaigns include using outside companies to push the government's priorities and messages in targeted adverts, which can take into account a person's age, gender, or location.

That could be inserting sponsored content on a person's social media feed in between posts from people they follow, or before a video on YouTube.

The FOI also reveals the unit has earmarked £750,000 for paying influencers to sell messages to their audiences, who may be mistrustful of a message coming directly from government.

One current campaign focused on the cost of living has paid content creators including Fisayo Martins, external, who runs a channel called Finance Matters UK on Instagram and TikTok, to advertise what support is available to citizens.

The Cabinet Office said the campaign has reached 13.2 million people on TikTok and 9.1 million people on Meta platforms, including Facebook and Instagram.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Angelina Jolie and Brad Pitt settle legal battle over French winery
BreakingNewsTab.text:
Brad Pitt and Angelina Jolie have settled a long-running legal battle over her sale of a stake in their French vineyard, which unfolded amid a bitter divorce.

"We have settled out of court in the best interests of our family and will not be commenting further," said the Hollywood stars' representatives in a joint statement.

They bought a controlling interest in Château Miraval in 2008 and wed there six years later.

In the lawsuit, Pitt, 62, argued that Jolie, 51, acted without his permission in selling her share in the winery to a Russian oligarch. She counter-sued, accusing Pitt of drunkenly attacking her and their children on a flight, prompting her to file for divorce in 2016.

The settlement announced on Wednesday resolves both of their respective legal actions.

"Any comments in media stories attributed to 'sources' are in fact not coming from either of us, or anyone close to us," said the statement from their representatives.

Pitt's lawsuit had accused Jolie of seeking "to inflict harm" on him when she sold her stake in their co-owned vineyard, which he claimed had forced him to partner with "a stranger with poisonous associations and intentions".

The Fight Club star said he and Jolie had agreed not to sell their stakes in the venue without the permission of the other.

It was alleged that Jolie had sold her share to a Luxembourg-based spirits manufacturer controlled by Russian oligarch Yuri Shefler, without Pitt's knowledge.

Jolie hit back with her own lawsuit, accusing Pitt of grabbing her by the head and attacking two of their children during a 2016 private jet flight trip.

Pitt also verbally abused and poured alcohol on his family during the flight from France to Los Angeles, her lawsuit had alleged.

Her lawyers alleged Pitt began shouting, accusing her of being "too deferential" to their six children - aged eight to 15 at the time.

Pitt was not charged following a police investigation into the incident and he denied the allegations.

They reached a divorce settlement late last year after an eight-year legal battle.

It is understood that Pitt's litigation with Stoli Group, a beverage company owned by the Russian oligarch, is ongoing.

BreakingNewsTab.title: UK Town of Culture: Strabane bid withdrawn over 'potential disaster for community relations'
BreakingNewsTab.text:
A competition that is supposed to celebrate local towns has been rejected by a council after it caused "great division" over its UK title.

The mainly-nationalist town of Strabane in County Tyrone was shortlisted as one of 15 possible locations for the inaugural UK Town of Culture 2028, with the chance to win £3m.

However, the local council voted not to go ahead with the bid on Wednesday with one councillor claiming it "has the potential to be a disaster for Strabane - for community relations".

The motion, which was put forward by independent councillors, was backed by the Social Democratic and Labour Party (SDLP) and Sinn Féin.

The council has to date spent around £40,000 on the bid.

A report prepared for councillors said that money had come from a £60,000 Department for Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) grant, and would need to be repaid if the bid did not make it to the final submission stage.

The competition is run by the DCMS.

Independent Paul Gallagher, who had previously expressed concerns about the town's entry in the competition, said it had "caused great division in Strabane town".

He said there was widespread concerns about the competition's UK title.

"If it was to go forward it would create a major distrust in this council among the residents of Strabane," said Gallagher.

Strabane, he said, would become "a very uncomfortable place" if the bid was progressed, adding there was the potential for protests in the town.

SDLP councillor Catherine McDaid said local concerns "need to be taken seriously".

"A cultural initiative should bring people together," she said.

"The priority now has to be to work on what has already been completed and looking into fresh opportunities for Strabane, shaped by what local people want and need, and grounded in their support," she said.

Ulster Unionist councillor Derek Hussey said it was "remiss" not to pursue with the bid.

Strabane and its people, he said, were being denied a similar opportunity to that of Derry which was the inaugural UK City of Culture in 2013.

Staying in the competition, he said, could "only be to the social and economic wellbeing of residents, business and visitors, long term as has been proved previously with the city's experience of having had the title of UK City of Culture," he said.

The Democratic Unionist Party's Keith Kerrigan said it was disappointing that at a time of wider investment in Strabane, the potential of a further £3m was being taken away.

"It is disappointing but we can see which way this vote is going to go," he said.

The council motion not to submit a final bid submission, included an amendment that council would work towards developing it s own cultural programme for the County Tyrone town in 2028.

The motion to not progress with the bid was first put forward last week at a council committee and was deferred until Wednesday's meeting.

At that time, councillors were told following two public engagement sessions in the town in early November, a total of 146 feedback forms were returned to council, six of which were supportive of the bid.

A further 140 forms voiced opposition to Strabane's entry.

BreakingNewsTab.title: Hera mission images from asteroid crash show stadium-sized crater
BreakingNewsTab.text:
The first images of an asteroid that Nasa deliberately crashed into have revealed a stadium-sized crater on its surface.

The extensive damage was caused when a Nasa spacecraft hit the asteroid Dimorphos in 2022. The asteroid posed no threat, but this was a test of our planetary defences to see if it was possible to knock a space rock off course.

Four years on, a European Space Agency (ESA) spacecraft called Hera is scouring the scene to fully assess the aftermath of the collision.

"The crater is almost as large as the body itself, which is really, really spectacular," said Dr Sabina Raducan, a planetary scientist, who is on the Hera science team.

"It's hard to describe in words all the excitement to actually finally see what happened. And as a crater person, I can also say it's beautiful."

The original 2022 crash test was carried out by a Nasa spacecraft called Dart which hurtled into Dimorphos at 14,000mph (22,000km/h).

It was such a big smash-up that the trail of debris, measuring about 6,200 miles long (10,000km), was spotted by telescopes on Earth and in space.

Dimorphos is about 150m (500ft) wide and was partly chosen as the target because it is one of an asteroid pair - it orbits around a larger space rock called Didymos, which is about 730m (2,400ft) wide.

The crash showed it was possible to change the path of the smaller asteroid.

Before the collision, it took Dimorphos 11 hours and 55 minutes to orbit around Didymos. After the crash, the duration of its orbit had shrunk by about 33 minutes.

A key objective of the Hera mission is to measure the mass of Dimorphos, in order to work out how effective the spacecraft's shove was.

This information would be vital if we ever spotted a space rock that was on a collision course with Earth.

"It would help us to predict what would happen if we had to hit another asteroid," said Prof Simon Green, a planetary scientist who is on Hera's science team.

"We [could] measure its properties and say: 'Well, we need this mass of spacecraft, travelling at this speed, this early, in order to deflect it enough so that it misses the Earth'."

Hera's arrival on the scene is helping scientists answer many more questions too.

Not only did the collision alter the shape of Dimorphos, it also changed the way it moves.

"Before the Dart impact, Dimorphos was more like our own Moon - so it was always showing the same face to Didymos, and it was behaving quite nicely," explained Raducan.

"Now it's very, very chaotic - it's tumbling. Imagine a barrel that you throw down the stairs, and the barrel is rolling and it's moving, and basically that's what Dimorphos does right now around Didymos."

Hera has also taken detailed images of Didymos, revealing its surface in detail.

"The gravity at the surface of Didymos is about 40,000 times less than the gravity on Earth," said Naomi Murdoch, who is on the Hera mission team.

"We can already see some fascinating and complex geology. We can see regions of boulders.

"The smallest details that we can make out in these images are about 3m in size. So that means that all the boulders that you can see with your eyes are at least 3m big, and some as big as 10m. So what we're seeing here is boulders the size of cars and buses sitting on a world with almost no gravity."

The Hera mission will spend the next six months studying Dimorphos and Didymos, sending back more images taken from closer up in higher resolution.

"Hera is a sort of Inspector Columbo going back to the crash scene to investigate what is the outcome of this impact," said Patrick Michel, principal investigator of ESA's Hera mission.

The spacecraft is packed with instruments and also has two shoebox-sized satellites on board, which can study the impact site up close and later land on the asteroid.

But the first images taken by Hera have also revealed a new challenge. Dimorphos and Didymos are travelling through space surrounded by hundreds of boulders ranging in size from tens of centimetres to metre-size rocks.

This will make it especially challenging to operate the spacecraft and cube satellites through this boulder field.

Scientists want to gather as much intelligence as they can about space rocks to make us as well equipped as possible to deal with whatever the Universe throws at us.

A new mission is launching in 2027 to track potentially hazardous asteroids - a space telescope called the Near-Earth Object (NEO) Surveyor.

There are also more visits planned to asteroids, including to one called Apophis, which is about 450m (1,480ft) long.

Apophis was discovered in 2004 and it was initially thought it might hit the Earth as early as 13 April 2029.

But now scientists understand its orbit better, and say it won't hit us for at least the next 100 years. Instead of a crash in 2029, it will fly just 32,000km (20,000 miles) above our surface.

This will give scientists the rare chance to study a space rock up-close.

Two spacecraft will head to Apophis, including Nasa's Osiris-Apex (which previously grabbed a sample from another asteroid called Bennu) and Ramses, a joint mission between ESA and the Japanese Space Agency (JAXA).

FinanceTab.title: Poundland collapses putting 11,000 jobs at risk
FinanceTab.text:
Poundland has collapsed into administration, putting 11,000 jobs at risk, after its owners failed to find a buyer to keep it in business.

The retailer's shops and distribution centres will remain open and continue to trade during the administration process with the business likely to be broken up and some of its stores sold off to rival retailers.

Poundland's US owners held talks with several bidders over a last-minute rescue deal, but no agreement was reached.

Poundland boss Barry Williams said in a note to staff that the board had "no alternative but to take this decision", but was making it with "sincere sadness and intense regret".

He said the US owners Gordon Brothers had removed "all borrowing facilities and access to our bank accounts" on 27 October, and adequate funds had not been released since then to keep the business solvent.

"Under these circumstances, it is impossible for the board of directors to see how Poundland can continue to operate as a going concern," he added.

Kelvin Blake, 62, who has worked for the firm for 25 years, and whose partner has been there 29 years, said he was feeling "down, depressed", and because of his age, feared he would not find a job elsewhere.

"We didn't want it, but it's come so now we've just got to face it and see what the future holds.

"My income's gone," he added. "Obviously, we'll be working until we're told to leave."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Poundland was "part of the fabric of high streets and communities up and down the country".

He said the news of it going into administration just weeks before Christmas would be "deeply concerning for workers and their families".

He added: "While it is worrying, going into administration does give other potential buyers the opportunity to engage and we will work hard with all the relevant parties to ensure the best possible outcome."

Alix Partners, which has been appointed as administrator, said they would look at all options for the business, "including sales of the business and its assets, either in whole or part".

"We appreciate this is a deeply concerning time for all involved - customers, suppliers and, in particular, Poundland colleagues," they said.

Gordon Brothers has been criticised over how it handled a potential sale of Poundland, with accusations the investment firm hoped to profit from selling off the chain's 600 shops and stock piecemeal after running it into the ground.

Gordon Brothers, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied such claims.

On the funding question, Gordon Brothers said it had loaned the firm £85m over a year to help save it from insolvency.

But insiders critical of the US firm have said it stands to make its loans back and more from the insolvency process.

Previously, Gordon Brothers netted millions from liquidating the stock of fashion retailer LK Bennett, and in insolvency fees.

Labour MP Liam Byrne told the BBC the House of Commons' Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee will recall Gordon Brothers before Parliament - two weeks after Gordon Brothers representatives last appeared at the committee to answer questions about Poundland, and where MPs said they were "deeply concerned" about the business.

Byrne said: "I am really worried that a 'greed is good' approach to business by its owners has forced [Poundland] into an administration."

He added the committee wants to know "how much money they're ripping out and crucially, how do we make sure, as a country, that we don't have this kind of scenario unfold again".

Gordon Brothers met Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds on Monday to update him on the progress.

The firm said on Wednesday that despite the Poundland management bringing about a turnaround over the past year, the firm was "still vulnerable" to inflation and any downturn in sales or profit margin, and it had faced "several years of instability".

A spokesperson added the firm's "thoughts are with Poundland colleagues".

It said it had stepped in to take over the retailer in 2025 when it was struggling, and when "no-one else was willing to finance the business".

One of the central stumbling blocks in negotiations to keep the business afloat was a shareholder loan Gordon Brothers inherited when it bought the business for less than £1 last year.

Gordon Brothers was owed £22.5m of that loan, while the previous owner Pepco was owed £7.5m.

Gordon Brothers rejected various offers to buy the business as a going concern with deals to pay off that loan.

Irish firm Martin Property Group offered to pay off £5m of the loan up front, and defer the rest of the payments to 2030.

London-based Xyra group offered £12.5m up front but ran out of time to get a deal over the line.

German investment firm Zachert Private Equity is also understood to have made a late offer.

All of these were rejected.

The crisis at Poundland really came to a head over the past few weeks after Gordon Brothers restricted access to funds for day-to-day operations.

This meant that stock at the retailer was not being replenished at the necessary pace in the vital run-up to the festive period.

FinanceTab.title: What's gone wrong at Poundland?
FinanceTab.text:
The future of Poundland hangs in the balance after the discount retailer's collapse into administration.

Its owner, US investment firm Gordon Brothers, put it up for sale in September, but then rejected offers to keep the business afloat.

Poundland has a major presence on the High Street, with 600 stores in the UK and Ireland, where it trades under the Dealz brand.

Its collapse puts the jobs of its 11,000 employees at risk, as well as potentially thousands of others at firms that supply the retailer.

How have we got here?

People have not stopped shopping at Poundland - quite the opposite.

Although the chain was struggling when it was sold by Pepco last year for £1, the business turned a corner over the year to September, going from a £68m loss to an £18.1m profit before interest, tax and certain accounting charges.

Going into the vital Christmas period, first-quarter like-for-like sales were up 7% and operational profits of £1.9m were up £1.2m on last year.

According to Julie Palmer, managing partner at insolvency specialist Begbies Traynor, "this isn't a story about shoppers abandoning Poundland".

She told the BBC the tills were "busier than they were a year ago", adding that on the face of it a turnaround seemed "well under way".

However, Gordon Brothers had been restricting Poundland's access to cash needed to restock stores and meet day-to-day expenses.

Poundland faced "a funding and ownership problem rather than a trading collapse", according to Palmer.

However, while Poundland boss Barry Williams claimed the business was making a "strong recovery", Gordon Brothers painted a different picture, saying the chain remained "challenged and vulnerable to any potential downturn in future trading".

It said it had provided significant funding to support the company's ability to trade since it acquired the business.

It has also made about £18m from a combination of debt interest payments and other fees and charges.

As well as being Poundland's owner, it is one of its lenders, and is owed loans, including a £22.5m shareholder loan it inherited when it bought the business for £1.

As the main creditor, Gordon Brothers would be first in line to get paid back if the business goes under - but its suppliers are not.

"When the owner is also the main lender, its first priority is recovering [loans]," says Palmer. "Sometimes the route that best protects the lender is different from the one that saves the most jobs, and that tension is why this has become such a political story."

Irish firm Martin Property Group, London-based holding company Xyra Group and German investment firm Zachert Private Equity are all also understood to have made offers for Poundland.

Gordon Brothers had also been weighing options to break Poundland up.

Its view was that ultimately breaking the retailer up would provide more security for employees in the long term, because any buyers of its store estate would also have to agree to keep the employees on.

Insiders who are critical of how Gordon Brothers has handled the Poundland sale accuse it of driving the business into the ground to make money through the insolvency process.

But the investment firm, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied the claim.

FinanceTab.title: US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China
FinanceTab.text:
The US has announced a fresh raft of tariffs as President Donald Trump pushes ahead with his signature trade policy.

The new taxes charged on imports to America are set to hit many of the country's biggest trading partners - China, the European Union and 12 other jurisdictions, including Japan, South Korea and Taiwan.

The White House began investigating the trade practices of other countries in March after the US Supreme Court ruled Trump's previously announced Liberation Day tariffs were illegal.

China is facing the highest tariff rate of up to 40%, followed by Vietnam at up to 35%, with others facing either 20% or 25%.

The US Trade Representative (USTR) announced the proposed tariffs together with extensive reports of how each jurisdiction's trade practices purportedly impact American commerce.

The new duties are not expected to take effect until next year and have to go through rounds of public consultation and, potentially, hearings.

Tariffs are taxes levied on imported goods. The amount is typically calculated as a percentage of a good's value and paid to the government by businesses importing products.

Some of these rates will be effectively reduced because of caps on tariffs Trump has agreed to. Individual countries also face different levies.

The proposed tariffs will affect goods from China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and India.

The USTR's Jamieson Greer said the latest tariffs issued would "level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy".

He said that many of America's trading partners had "for decades" adopted industrial strategies which included "targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression".

They also employ "other market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favour while eroding America's manufacturing base", Greer said.

But economists have warned tariffs can fuel inflation and push prices up for consumers if businesses pass on higher costs, as well as dampen global trade.

Trump has repeatedly threatened or imposed tariffs during his second term, arguing they will boost US manufacturing and create jobs.

Despite a poor result for the Republican party in the midterm elections, the president has continued to press on with his flagship trade policy.

Trump is also seeking to cut the US trade deficit - the gap between the value of goods it buys from other countries and those it sells to them.

These new levies are build on a "stronger legal foundation" under US law compared with Trump's April 2025 Liberation Day tariffs, Singapore Management University economics lecturer Chang Pao-Li said.

Trump previously invoked emergency presidential powers to impose tariffs that have since been struck down, while his latest approach relies on the USTR's authority to impose tariffs to address certain foreign trade practices, she said.

The levies are still likely to face legal challenges, but there has been a "historical precedent" for such tariffs remaining in force, Chang said.

Many tariffs imposed under Section 301 - a law that allows the US to probe and retaliate against foreign trade practices - during Trump's first term remained in effect during his successor Joe Biden's administration.

However, Stephen Brown, chief North America economist for Capital Economics, said the latest tariff announcement was "not as alarming as it looks", due to the taxes "essentially replacing" previously announced tariffs made in the summer.

"The increase in the effective tariff rate looks set to be a touch lower than we've been assuming for our forecasts, although the new tariffs will still provide a marginal boost to prices," he said in a note.

The additional tariff burden is likely to be small because a limited number of goods are subject to the new duties, Brown added.

Jurisdictions affected by the new wave of tariffs have voiced their disapproval over the Trump administration's move.

Washington has also proposed a 10% tariff on goods from Brazil, as part of a separate investigation over what it says are "harmful trade practices" undercutting American workers.

Brazilian authorities expressed their "outrage" at the announcement, saying that the move is aimed at pressuring the government to change regulations around issues like digital trade.

The South American nation faces duties on finished aircraft and sugar sold to the US.

"Brazil will not yield to such threats," President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva's office said.

The European Commission rejected the new US tariffs, saying it would investigate the reasons for bringing them in. It pointed out that tariffs are limited to the 15% previously agreed.

The latest tariff rate is "not consistent" with the reality of bilateral economic-trade cooperation between the US and Vietnam, Vietnamese Deputy Prime Minister Bui Thanh Son said.

The Japanese government said the US tariffs were "regrettable", while the Singapore government said it disagrees with the White House's findings and that it is engaging the USTR to explore ways to reduce the tariff.

South Korea's trade minister said the proposed 15% tariff will be "more than a decent outcome" as it would fall in line with a previously agreed limit with Washington.

Last year, Seoul pledged $350bn (£267bn) in US investments in exchange for lower tariffs as part of a trade deal.

US trading partners have been "waiting for this shoe to drop" and have argued that they are being wrongly accused of producing too much, said the Asia Society Policy Institute's Wendy Cutler, a former senior US trade negotiator.

"Many believe that China, not them, should be the target for US action," she added.

Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun described the new tariffs as a form of "political manipulation", describing as "false" the US claim that China produces more than it can consume.

The tariff announcement is likely to increase tensions between the US and China, the world's two biggest economies, who remain locked in a trade dispute and the AI race.

The two countries have also been embroiled in a tit-for-tat tariffs war, which is currently on hold.

Despite last week's meeting between Trump and China's President Xi Jinping, the two sides made no announcement on the trade war truce, which is set to expire on 10 January.

Beijing has remained vague on how it will respond but for now seems "prepared to live with the new rates provided they don't exceed 20%", Cutler said.

Additional reporting by Leehyun Choi in Seoul

FinanceTab.title: US stocks fall further as fears over AI intensify
FinanceTab.text:
Big technology firms connected to AI continued to see share prices fall on Wednesday, with stock in Nvidia and Anthropic dropping sharply in early trading.

The surge in Nvidia shares after boss Jensen Huang was reinstated was temporary, and the general stock sell-off continued, with all three main US stock market indices down by closing time. The tech-dominated Nasdaq closed 0.6% lower.

The declines came amid concerns over the level and sustainability of AI investment, which has rattled investors in recent weeks.

Shares in other major tech firms, including Amazon, Tesla and Microsoft closed the day lower, though Meta and SpaceX were in positive territory by the end of the trading day.

Nvidia's share price was down 8% in early trading on Wednesday, extending Tuesday's slide as the boost from Huang's return eased. At close, it ended up 3.4% lower.

The resignation and subsequent reinstatement of Nvidia's CEO after revelations of his extramarital affairs has seen the market value of the world's premier AI chipmaker fluctuate wildly.

Given Nvidia's position as both supplier and financier of many other firms involved in the AI rollout, its rocky fortnight has had a wider impact.

The US government also announced a raft of new tariffs on countries and trading partners on Wednesday as part of President Donald Trump's flagship trade policy.

The value of big tech companies have sheltered the US economy from global economic shocks, including tariffs.

But share prices in recent weeks have been volatile in response to the US midterm elections and other events in the AI industry.
